_about: The retrieval shelf for pages/chart-lab.html (a mock-up). Built by scripts/build_chart_lab_passages.py from the school grammars in grammars/, short windows of the public-domain books in sources/public-domain (<= 60 words, archive.org search-inside links) and podcast auto-caption snippets (<= 20 words, linked to the YouTube moment, no episode titles). No chart and no personal data. No text of Bailey's Esoteric Astrology: that school is our own paraphrase grammar.

sections.Interpretation: The pioneer of the zodiac. Aries represents the outrushing of spirit into matter, the primal will to exist. Those born under this sign possess courage, enterprise, and the power to initiate. The Aries nature is direct, frank, and fearless, with strong executive ability. The higher type shows the spiritual warrior, fighting for principle rather than personal gain.
sections.Light: The spiritual warrior—courage devoted to principle, leadership that inspires others to action.
sections.Shadow: Selfishness, impatience, the lower martial nature that fights for personal gain alone.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: This sign governs the head and face, hence the consciousness making the character of the Aries individual will always express itself through the head; this sign is the head of the fiery triplicity, and belongs to the cardinal signs. We find persons born under the rule of this sign always looking forward, they are leaders in ideals and pioneers of advanced thought. They have great mental energy but are inclined to be very headstrong and impulsive. They are always prophetic, and love to predict things that will …

sections.Interpretation: The builder and stabilizer. Taurus represents the desire nature seeking permanent form. Those born here possess determination, patience, and practical ability. The Taurus nature is steady, reliable, and appreciative of beauty and comfort. The higher type transmutes possessiveness into stewardship, using material resources for spiritual purposes.
sections.Light: The spiritual steward—using material resources for higher purposes, building forms that serve the soul.
sections.Shadow: Possessiveness, materialism, stubborn attachment to forms that have outlived their purpose.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: This sign is the first of the earthy triplicity and the first of the fixed signs, and in this sign is concealed will and desire, both of which express themselves, more or less, in the character of the Taureans. This being the sign of solidity it makes those born in it exceedingly solid, practical, and substantial. They are exactly the reverse of all that has been said in the foregoing sign, Aries being all that is idealistic, while Taurus is all that is practical. The Taureans are slow, plodding, patient …

sections.Interpretation: The messenger and communicator. Gemini represents the reasoning mind seeking to understand duality. Those born here possess versatility, intellectual curiosity, and the gift of expression. The Gemini nature is alert, adaptable, and forever seeking new knowledge. The higher type unifies the lower and higher mind, becoming a channel for wisdom.
sections.Light: The divine messenger—unifying lower and higher mind, channeling wisdom through intellect.
sections.Shadow: Superficiality, scattered attention, the lower mind that gathers without synthesizing.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: This is the first sign of the airy triplicity, also the first of the mutable signs. The airy triplicity governs the mental conditions of humanity, hence we find those born in this sign living more in the mind, but, owing to the sign belonging to the mutable group, they are dualistic — this being the main feature of the mutable signs, and from this comes the tendency to express two conditions and an inclination at times to be rather easily influenced on one side or the other. Gemini governs the lungs, also the …

sections.Interpretation: The mother of the zodiac. Cancer represents the soul seeking incarnation through feeling and memory. Those born here possess sensitivity, tenacity, and deep protective instincts. The Cancer nature is receptive, nurturing, and connected to the past. The higher type becomes the universal mother, extending care beyond personal attachments.
sections.Light: The universal mother—extending nurturing care beyond personal attachments to all who need it.
sections.Shadow: Moodiness, clinging to the past, emotional manipulation through guilt or need.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: The sign Cancer begins the maternal trinity. It is the first of the watery triplicity and the second of the cardinal signs. This sign governs the breast and stomach. It is one of the most sensitive signs of the zodiac, and belonging as it does to the maternal trinity, it governs all home and domestic affairs in which the feelings play a prominent part. Persons born in this sign are characterised as being slow but sure. They are best described by the crab, whose tenacity is proverbial; this creature moves forward …

sections.Interpretation: The king and creator. Leo represents the individualized self seeking expression and recognition. Those born here possess dignity, generosity, and natural authority. The Leo nature is warm, dramatic, and magnanimous when evolved. The higher type rules through love rather than dominion, radiating light that elevates others.
sections.Light: The benevolent ruler—leading through love, radiating light that elevates all it touches.
sections.Shadow: Pride, arrogance, the need for constant recognition, dominion rather than service.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Leo is the middle sign of the maternal trinity, the second of the fiery triplicity, and also the second of the fixed signs, therefore it may be said to hold the central point in the zodiac… Leo governs the heart, therefore it will be from this centre that the character of those born in this sign must be judged. … generally speaking, the emotions are fully active in the Leo characters. They are forceful and highly magnetic, and possessing an abundance of vitality, they carry with them an aura that is beneficial to …

sections.Interpretation: The craftsman and servant. Virgo represents the discriminating mind perfecting form through service. Those born here possess analytical ability, practical skill, and dedication to improvement. The Virgo nature is modest, methodical, and health-conscious. The higher type serves humanity selflessly, finding divinity in the details of daily work.
sections.Light: The sacred servant—finding divinity in details, perfecting form as an act of devotion.
sections.Shadow: Criticism, worry, perfectionism that paralyzes rather than refines.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: The sign Virgo is the second of the earthy triplicity, the second of the mutable signs, and the turning-point from the northern to the southern signs. This sign is specially characterised for its self-containing qualities; it is out of this sign that wisdom is to be born for the majority of individualities. … The individuals born in this sign are constructive and able to make the most of their conditions; they are more generally found in the business world, particularly in pursuits which provide for the general …

sections.Interpretation: The harmonizer and judge. Libra represents the soul seeking equilibrium through relationship. Those born here possess diplomacy, artistic sense, and the desire for justice. The Libra nature is refined, cooperative, and peace-loving. The higher type achieves inner balance that no longer depends on external harmony, becoming a true peacemaker.
sections.Light: The true peacemaker—achieving inner balance that radiates outward, justice tempered by love.
sections.Shadow: Indecision, dependence on others for equilibrium, peace-keeping that avoids necessary conflict.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Libra, the sign of the balance, the equalising sign of the zodiac, is the second of the airy triplicity, and the third of the cardinal signs. The individuality of this sign is expressed in justice, equilibrium, balance, order and dispassionate judgment. Those born in this sign are remarkable for their powers of comparison; they seem to be able to weigh and balance all things mentally, as though they were inspired. Extremes may be found in this sign as in all the cardinal signs, but sooner or later opportunities …

sections.Interpretation: The transformer and regenerator. Scorpio represents the emotional nature confronting death and rebirth. Those born here possess intensity, resourcefulness, and penetrating insight. The Scorpio nature is passionate, secretive, and powerfully magnetic. The higher type transmutes personal desire into spiritual will, becoming the eagle that soars above the serpent.
sections.Light: The eagle—transmuting desire into will, using emotional power for transformation and healing.
sections.Shadow: The scorpion—jealousy, revenge, using emotional intensity to manipulate or destroy.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Scorpio is the third of the fixed signs and the second or middle of the watery triplicity. Its symbol is known as the scorpion, whose sting becomes the most prominent feature in evolving through this sign. We may find characters born in this sign from the lowest and most degraded to the highest and most exalted, and in this sign there appears to be more scope for extremes of character than in any other. The Scorpio character is somewhat decided and unmistakable, being rarely, if ever, vacillating or feeble. … When …

sections.Interpretation: The philosopher and seeker. Sagittarius represents the higher mind aspiring toward truth and meaning. Those born here possess enthusiasm, optimism, and love of freedom. The Sagittarian nature is jovial, adventurous, and prophetic. The higher type becomes the true teacher, pointing the way to wisdom while respecting each soul's unique path.
sections.Light: The true teacher—pointing toward wisdom while honoring each soul's unique journey.
sections.Shadow: Dogmatism, restlessness, the preacher who imposes rather than inspires.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Sagittarius is the sign of the archer, who stands ready to shoot from his bow the arrow which is said to never fail in hitting the mark, which means that they have the power of prophecy for their special feature. There is an idea of freedom conveyed in the symbol of the archer, and of these individuals it may be said that they always aim for the highest. … Sagittarius is the last of the fiery triplicity and the third of the mutable signs; it therefore represents the union of qualities of the head and heart, now …

sections.Interpretation: The father and administrator. Capricorn represents ambition crystallizing into achievement through discipline. Those born here possess endurance, organizational ability, and respect for tradition. The Capricorn nature is serious, responsible, and ambitious. The higher type uses worldly position for spiritual service, becoming the initiate who has mastered matter.
sections.Light: The initiate—using mastery of matter for spiritual service, worldly position devoted to higher purpose.
sections.Shadow: Cold ambition, materialism, using structure to control rather than to serve.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Capricorn is the last of the cardinal signs, and also the last of the earthy triplicity and the first of what is well termed the serving trinity. … The Capricornians, when individualised, are impartial, just and accurate, aiming to be precise, exact and constant, fulfilling all things with a persistent, persevering and industrious nature. They are assiduous, arduous and careful, zealous and diligent, ever enduring with a calm, earnest patience, and a grave reflective demeanour. They seem to have brought the …

sections.Interpretation: The humanitarian and reformer. Aquarius represents the universal mind working for collective progress. Those born here possess originality, humanitarian ideals, and scientific ability. The Aquarian nature is independent, progressive, and oriented toward the future. The higher type serves humanity through brotherhood, seeing all as equal expressions of the one life.
sections.Light: The world server—seeing all as equal expressions of one life, working for humanity's progress.
sections.Shadow: Emotional detachment, eccentricity for its own sake, ideas divorced from human feeling.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: Aquarius is the last of the airy triplicity, also the last of the fixed signs and the centre of the serving trinity. … Its symbol is the man commonly known as the water-bearer… Aquarian individuals are determined, patient, quiet, unobtrusive and faithful. They have the power of concentrating their thoughts, and are generally philosophic and scientific. They lead toward the unconventional, and thus become excellent reformers; they have bright and clear intellects, and persevere patiently with all their pursuits. …

sections.Interpretation: The mystic and redeemer. Pisces represents the soul completing its cycle, dissolving separateness through compassion. Those born here possess imagination, sensitivity, and spiritual receptivity. The Piscean nature is gentle, impressionable, and self-sacrificing. The higher type becomes the conscious server, willingly taking on the suffering of others to aid their liberation.
sections.Light: The conscious server—willingly bearing others' suffering to aid liberation, redeeming through love.
sections.Shadow: Victimhood, escapism, losing self in others' pain without the strength to transform it.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (Astrology for All: This is the last sign of the zodiac, the sign of the fishes. It is the last of the watery and mutable signs. Its symbol represents two fishes tied together, one swimming in one direction and the other in the opposite. … There can be no such thing as a real failure; but if we were to think of a progression through all the signs, and then think of the sign Pisces as representing, on the one hand, those who had succeeded in extracting the virtue from each, and, on the other hand, those who had failed to accomplish …

sections.Interpretation: The Sun represents the immortal Individuality, the divine spark within. It shows what we are becoming through evolution, our essential spiritual nature. In the horoscope, a strong Sun indicates one who can express their true self with power and authority. The Sun is the life-giver, and its position shows where we must shine.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The Sun, we are taught by those who are seeking the Path of Wisdom, is the body of God, the Logos of this solar system, through which He gives His Love, Light and Life. In astrologic study the Sun gives to every living organism its Prāna, or life and heat, each individual specialising his own store from the cosmic Prāna. Every living thing is plunged into a great ocean of life — God's life; and every organism, whether great or small, appropriates to itself some of this universal life which is ever flowing from the …

sections.Interpretation: The Moon represents the Personality, the sum of past experiences carried into this life. It shows our habits, instincts, and automatic responses—what we have been. The Moon governs the physical body, the public, women, and all matters of common everyday life. Its position shows our receptive, feeling nature.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The Moon acts as the vehicle, or link of communication between the Sun and each living thing. In Astrology the Moon is the representation of the Personality, the portion of the individual that is manifested during the one life period, and as such the Moon's position and aspects become the most important when judging a nativity. If the Moon has no aspect whatever with the Sun, or is in much affliction with this luminary, then the life forces do not flow evenly, the mentality is not so sharp and clear, and the …

sections.Interpretation: Mercury represents the rational mind, the link between higher and lower self. It governs communication, learning, and the nervous system. Mercury shows how we think, speak, and process information. Well-aspected, it gives intellectual brilliance; afflicted, it produces worry and nervous disorders.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Mercury is known as the 'convertible' planet. It is neither positive nor negative, but both. It is the planet of the adept, being the planet of adaptation in the widest sense of the word. Mercury is termed the Winged Messenger of the Gods, and takes upon himself the vibrations of all the other planets. It is, in one word, the planet of Reason. In the physical world Mercury governs the sense of seeing. It has also a very close relationship with the mind. … It has also a subjective as well as an objective influence …

sections.Interpretation: Venus represents the love nature, attraction, and the desire for harmony. It governs art, beauty, social relations, and values. Venus shows what we love and find beautiful. Well-aspected, it gives charm and artistic ability; afflicted, it produces excessive pleasure-seeking or difficulty in relationships.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The two benefic planets are Venus and Jupiter. Venus and Jupiter are the respective counterparts of Mars and Saturn… The only real difference between these two planets, Mars and Venus, arises from the special vibrations. Mars is attracted from without through desire and impulse. Venus causes all action to come from within, and instead of feeling rushing outwards to objects and becoming captive to externals, it moves from within through the ego's direct intuitive power. The vibrations of Venus directly affect the …

sections.Interpretation: Mars represents the desire nature, courage, and the power to act. It governs physical energy, competition, and the sexual drive. Mars shows how we assert ourselves and fight for what we want. Well-aspected, it gives courage and enterprise; afflicted, it produces anger, accidents, and strife.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Mars is the planet of focussed force, and out-going impulse. Physical heat and motion are more under the direct influence of Mars than any other planet. He governs the sense of taste in its widest application. All the animal propensities, sensations, passions, desires and appetites come under the vibration of Mars. … Force and energy are at all times necessary on the physical plane, and without the martial influence humanity would be tame and inactive, therefore use will make the vibrations of Mars as beneficial …

sections.Interpretation: Jupiter represents the higher mind, faith, and the principle of growth. It governs philosophy, religion, law, and long journeys. Jupiter shows where we seek meaning and where fortune smiles upon us. Well-aspected, it gives wisdom and prosperity; afflicted, it produces excess, extravagance, and false optimism.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Jupiter is termed the Greater Fortune. Its vibrations are concerned with the form side of manifestation and like Saturn it symbolises the vehicle which holds the life. … Saturn contracts and acts microscopically. Jupiter expands and has no limit to its expansion. Mind and feeling are condensed and focussed in the limiting form of Saturn, and expanded, broadened, and extended through the ever-increasing form of Jupiter. In these two extremes we have all the elements of pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow, increase …

sections.Interpretation: Saturn represents karma, discipline, and the lessons of time. It governs structure, responsibility, and crystallization. Saturn shows where we must work hard and accept limitation. Well-aspected, it gives stability and achievement; afflicted, it produces fear, delay, and depression. Saturn is the great teacher.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The next so-called evil planet is Saturn. The nature and influence of this planet is cold and binding, exactly opposite to that of the fiery Mars. … Saturn governs the sense of hearing, a negative or receptive sense. The listener suggests patience, forbearance, silence and caution. The planetary vibration of Saturn restricts, limits, crystallises and binds everything; holding, restraining, fashioning and solidifying all that comes under its sphere of influence. … It is therefore the vibrations of Saturn that cause …

sections.Interpretation: Uranus represents the higher will, sudden change, and liberation from the past. It governs originality, invention, and revolution. Uranus shows where we break free from convention and express our uniqueness. Its influence is sudden, unexpected, and often disruptive to the status quo.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The planet Uranus has less influence at the present day than any other planet except Neptune. It is the planet of the coming race, for its vibrations will then be more important than to-day. It is thought by the author to represent the fully individualised Ego, and as such is the houseless wanderer half-way between earth and heaven. Its vibrations are different from those of any other planet, governing all things that are not bound by convention or limited entirely to the form side of things… It appears to govern …

sections.Interpretation: Neptune represents the higher love, inspiration, and the dissolution of boundaries. It governs mysticism, dreams, and the unseen realms. Neptune shows where we transcend ordinary consciousness. Well-aspected, it gives spiritual vision; afflicted, it produces confusion, deception, and escapism.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Neptune, the last discovered planet, has, on the whole, but a faint influence upon our earth and its inhabitants. The undeveloped psychic who is unable to control the mediumistic tendencies induced from without, and those who are easily obsessed or of very weak will, always subject to changing impressions, will in one sense come under Neptune as will also those who are very highly advanced psychically. Experience tends to prove that the influence of an afflicted Neptune as a rule is undesirable. There is a …

sections.Interpretation: The house of the physical body and personal appearance. It represents the mask we wear, our approach to life, and how others see us. Planets here strongly color the personality and physical constitution.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The sign, and more especially the particular degree, of the zodiac rising upon the eastern horizon at birth is known as the Ascendant. This term also embraces the whole of the first house… The ascendant rules the personal appearance and to a considerable extent also the health, mind, and disposition. It is that part of the horoscope which has more to do with the physical body and its material wants than any other portion. The five physical senses find their outlet through this ascendant, and much depends upon the …

sections.Interpretation: The house of money, possessions, and personal values. It shows our attitude toward material security and what we value. The second house reveals our earning capacity and relationship with the material world.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: In any horoscope money matters are judged largely, but not exclusively, from the state of the second house. As we have seen elsewhere, this house belongs to the triad of tenth, second and sixth: and of these the tenth house or mid-heaven is concerned to a great extent with occupation, business, profession; the sixth with servants, employees, situations, positions or spheres of activity in which money may be earned; and the second with money. In addition, the eighth house has to do with money inherited, legacies …

sections.Interpretation: The house of the concrete mind, communication, and immediate environment. It governs siblings, neighbors, short journeys, and early education. This house shows how we think and express our thoughts.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The First House has a very decided influence over the physical body as a whole, governing what we may term the general temperament. The Second House has also a decided influence in this respect, having considerable sway over the emotional and desire nature. The Third House in the same way has a definite influence over the mind; these three houses analogically coming under the dominant rulership of the three planets Mars, Venus and Mercury respectively. In the Third House, which we are now to consider, we study all …

sections.Interpretation: The house of home, family, and psychological foundations. It represents one parent, our roots, and the end of life. The fourth house shows our deepest private self and sense of security.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The fourth house relates to the 'grave,' the end of life, one of the parents — usually the father, according to Western astrologers, though the Hindus say the mother, since the fourth house corresponds to Cancer — and denotes also the environment, residence and family conditions in which the native dwells. … The fourth house may be briefly summarised as the personal environment, the tenth house as the individual environment. … the fourth house represents in a general sense the centre or focus of the personal or …

sections.Interpretation: The house of self-expression, creativity, and pleasure. It governs children, romance, speculation, and amusements. This house shows how we express our creative power and find joy.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The fifth house relates to pleasure, society and social inclinations, also the emotions and feelings. It may be regarded as a material representation of the eleventh house, which governs hopes and wishes, and often denotes their worldly fulfilment. It shows the nature of the native's love affairs, courtships, and the affections which spring from the feeling and emotional side of the nature; it represents the seat of the physical and magnetic attractions between the sexes. It is also concerned with speculative …

sections.Interpretation: The house of health, work, and service. It governs employment, daily routine, and small animals. This house shows our attitude toward duty and the care of the physical body.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The sixth house is connected with the mid-heaven and the second house and relates to work and servants, also to sickness, and the condition of the physical body. It is an unimportant house if no planets are found in it, or if the sign upon the cusp has no definite indication relating to sixth house affairs. In some cases it is necessary to study the ruler of this house, but only when so placed or aspected as to show marked signs of importance. In all cases where a planet occupies this house it will have some …

sections.Interpretation: The house of marriage, partnership, and open enemies. It represents our approach to committed relationships and what we seek in others. This house shows how we relate one-to-one.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Marriage is the chief influence of the seventh house. The seventh house in every horoscope is the complement of the first, and represents the unifying of all that is separated or isolated in the ascendant; it indicates the subjective side of the nature as distinguished from the objective side indicated by the first house: and successfully to unify all that is denoted by the first and seventh means an enlarged experience which can be gained in no other way. In the abstract, it means the blending of Mars and Venus …

sections.Interpretation: The house of death, transformation, and shared resources. It governs inheritance, the occult, and deep psychological change. This house shows our capacity for rebirth and handling of others' resources.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: This house belongs to the triangle of fourth, eighth, and twelfth; which have as their correspondences Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces, ruled by the Moon, Mars and Jupiter. These form the watery, psychic, or astral subdivision of the zodiac and indicate channels through which influences (good or bad) may flow down upon the man from the next interior plane of being, as well as ways by which he may himself contact that plane. Of these three, the eighth house is generally considered to have a direct bearing upon death and …

sections.Interpretation: The house of the higher mind, religion, and long journeys. It governs philosophy, law, publishing, and foreign cultures. This house shows our search for meaning and expansion of consciousness.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The ninth house is the house of philosophy, the higher mind, and hence of all that concerns the scientific and religious attitude of the native. It is the house of the subjective and abstract mind as opposed to the objective and concrete brain mind, represented by the third house. The third house, representing the smaller and slower mind which has its range in the physical world only, also represents short journeys and travelling by land; while the ninth house, signifying the wider and less limited mind, also …

sections.Interpretation: The house of career, reputation, and public standing. It represents one parent, authority figures, and our ambitions. This house shows our contribution to society and how we're known publicly.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: This is the house of honour, reputation, profession, business or occupation, and represents the public standing or worldly position of the native. It may be taken as the apex of the horoscope, or that portion which is thrust out most prominently into the busy life of the world. Good and evil must both alike find expression, and culminate in honour or dishonour; and the culminating point is the tenth house. An action may be said to be the child of thought and desire, which are its parents. The impulse to action …

sections.Interpretation: The house of friends, groups, and hopes. It governs social circles, humanitarian interests, and our wishes for the future. This house shows how we participate in collective endeavors.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: This house is that of friends, acquaintances, hopes, wishes, aspirations. It belongs to the triangle of the seventh and third houses, and has a great deal in common with both of these. By secondary influence it stands to the seventh house as the fifth stands to the first; that is, it is the fifth house of the marriage partner, and therefore has to be taken into account when considering questions concerning children and the other affairs of the fifth house. Taken by itself, free from affliction, it may be …

sections.Interpretation: The house of seclusion, karma, and self-undoing. It governs hospitals, prisons, hidden enemies, and the unconscious. This house shows our hidden strengths and weaknesses, and the soul's need for retreat.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The twelfth house is generally supposed to be the house of sorrow, enemies, imprisonment and misfortune. This is probably owing to its being one of the houses belonging to the psychic trinity; and, as the cadent houses of that triangle, it is the least fortunate of the three. … The Cardinal houses or 'Angles' represent the physical body, and all that is expressed by action in the outer or external world; they are quick, acute, active, energetic, open. … The Succedent houses are less physical and material in their …

sections.Interpretation: A blending and intensification of planetary energies. The conjunction unites two principles for good or ill depending on the planets involved. It represents a new beginning, a seed point of concentrated force.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: Conjunction is when two heavenly bodies are together at the same point of the zodiac. It therefore stands, symbolically if not practically, for union, synthesis, the blending of two in one. What effect the union will have depends upon the nature of the combined planets. When two forces meet, the resultant varies according to the angle between them and the strength of each force. When two notes are sounded together upon a musical instrument, the resulting sound depends upon whether the two sets of vibrations …

sections.Interpretation: An aspect of opportunity and talent. The sextile indicates natural abilities that can be developed with effort. It represents harmonious cooperation between planetary principles.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The formation of these aspects will be made clear to the mind by the following illustration. At the time of the New Moon, the Moon and Sun are in conjunction, i.e., they occupy the same degree of the zodiac, but as the Moon moves faster than the Sun, they very soon separate, and in fact two-and-a-half days later the Moon is 30° further on in the zodiac than the Sun is, and five days later 60° further on; hence they are said to be respectively in 'semi-sextile' and in 'sextile' to each other at these dates. … The …

sections.Interpretation: An aspect of friction and challenge. The square creates tension that demands action and growth. It represents obstacles that build character when overcome.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The Evil Aspects represent the circle halved or quartered. Thus the opposition, 180°, is half the circle, the square, 90°, is a quarter of the circle, and the semi-square, 45°, and sesquiquadrate, 135°, are respectively half a square and a square and a half. … Of the evil aspects, the Opposition and Square may be compared to Saturn and Mars respectively. The opposition separates, and causes rivalry, antagonism, duality, in this respect being not unlike the mutable signs in its influence. The square acts somewhat …

sections.Interpretation: An aspect of ease and natural flow. The trine indicates gifts and talents that express effortlessly. It represents harmony between planetary principles, though it may produce complacency.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The Good Aspects are all based upon a threefold division of the circle of the zodiac. Thus the trine, 120°, is a third of the circle… The religious philosophy of the mystic assures us that there is a basic three-fold mode of operation underlying the whole universe, and that it can be stated in terms of consciousness and in terms of force working through matter. … We are apparently justified in conjecturing that the angle of 120° harmonises with the material constitution of the solar system and with the modes of …

sections.Interpretation: An aspect of awareness through polarity. The opposition creates tension between opposing principles that must be balanced. It represents the need to integrate seemingly contradictory energies through relationship.
sections.The record — Alan Leo (How to Judge a Na: The opposition aspect is when two planets are situated at exactly opposite points in the zodiac. Let us suppose that these are Venus and Mars. In this case the soul and the senses will be at war and the person will suffer. He will find it a hard task to preserve a straight course morally through life; his passions will be continually overstepping the bounds of moderation, especially in the direction of sex. When he truly realises this, and that it is a highly undesirable phase of character, he will have made a big …

passages.name: Uranus

sections.Archetype: In Tarnas's archetypal astrology, Uranus is the Promethean principle — the impulse that breaks a pattern before it hardens into a cage. Where Saturn conserves what already exists, Uranus is the sudden opening: the idea that arrives all at once, the revolution that will not wait for permission, the moment a settled order is startled into something it did not choose. Tarnas reads Uranus transits as correlating with awakening, individuation, and rupture — genius, invention, and liberation on one face; disruption …

sections.Archetype: Neptune, for Tarnas, is dissolution itself — the archetypal current that erodes the boundary between self and world, waking and dream, the literal and the symbolic. It is the oceanic: mysticism, music, compassion, and imagination at its most numinous, and, on its shadow side, illusion, addiction, deception, and the fog in which nothing quite holds its shape. Tarnas treats Neptune transits as correlating with periods when the given world softens — utopian longing, spiritual opening, collective idealism — and with …

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Pluto

sections.Archetype: Pluto, in Tarnas's account, is the underworld drive — elemental, compulsive, and largely unconscious until it isn't. It is the id in the oldest sense: instinct, sexuality, mortality, and the will to power, all the material a settled ego would rather not look at directly. Tarnas reads Pluto transits as correlating with death-and-rebirth intensities — destruction that clears ground, and the regeneration that can only happen once something has actually ended. Its gift is depth; its danger is that depth, unintegrated …

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Sun

sections.Archetype: The Sun, in the broader archetypal-astrology tradition Tarnas works within, is the will-to-be-oneself — the organizing center around which a life composes itself, the light a person recognizes as unmistakably theirs. Its gift is vitality: purpose, self-expression, the courage to occupy the center of one's own story. Its shadow is the same gesture turned rigid — an ego that mistakes shining for being seen, or burns itself and everyone nearby chasing significance. Tarnas's own signature method reads planetary pairs …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, the Sun is core identity — conscious will, creative force, the organizing principle a life composes itself around. Its light is vitality, self-expression, and generous leadership; its shadow, an ego that inflates or burns itself out chasing achievement. The Sun's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Moon

sections.Archetype: The Moon is the soul's own weather — memory, feeling, the wordless knowing that shapes a person before language does. It governs receptivity: the capacity to be moved, held, and to hold in turn, the tidal rhythm underneath a life's more visible ambitions. Its gift is attunement, an instinct for what a moment or a person actually needs. Its shadow is the tide with no shore: moods that flood a room, a need for safety so large it swallows the person feeling it. Tarnas's own signature method reads planetary pairs …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, the Moon is the emotional body — how you feel, what you need, where you seek comfort — governing instinct, memory, home, and nurture. Its light is receptivity, intuition, and emotional intelligence; its shadow, moodiness, dependency, and a clinging to the past. The Moon's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Mercury

sections.Archetype: Mercury is the connective principle — the quick, curious intelligence that moves between things and makes them speak to each other: thought, language, the nervous system's own restlessness. Its gift is the exact word, the useful question, a mind agile enough to translate one world into another. Its shadow is that same quickness turned glib — cleverness without depth, information without understanding, a trickster's charm used to dodge rather than connect. Tarnas's outer-planet correlations are his signature …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, Mercury is the mind in motion — thought, language, learning, and the bridges between things. Its light is curiosity, adaptability, and the exact word; its shadow, overthinking, scattered attention, and the trickster's glibness. Mercury's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Venus

sections.Archetype: Venus is the drive toward relatedness — the pull to find what is beautiful, to be drawn toward another, to want harmony enough to build it. It governs eros in its gentler register: attraction, aesthetic pleasure, the values a person will actually organize a life around. Its gift is the capacity to love well and to make things worth loving. Its shadow is relatedness curdled into vanity, or a peace purchased by avoiding every real conflict. Tarnas's own signature work is the collective, historical reading of …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, Venus is what you love, what you value, and how you attract — beauty, pleasure, relationship, and the principle of harmony. Her light is grace, magnetism, and devotion; her shadow, vanity, possessiveness, and a peace kept by pleasing everyone. Venus's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Mars

sections.Archetype: Mars is assertive desire — the will that acts, the edge between wanting something and going to get it. It is eros's more combative twin: courage, initiative, the readiness to fight for what matters, including oneself. Its gift is aliveness with teeth, the energy that actually moves a life forward instead of merely wishing it would. Its shadow is that same force turned careless or cruel: aggression without aim, a temper that mistakes domination for strength. Tarnas reads Mars mostly inside larger complexes — paired …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, Mars is drive, desire, and fighting spirit — how you assert yourself, pursue what you want, and meet conflict. Its light is courage, initiative, and decisiveness; its shadow, aggression, impatience, and recklessness. Mars's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Jupiter

sections.Archetype: Jupiter is the expansive principle — the impulse toward more: more meaning, more possibility, more room to grow into. It governs faith in the largest sense, the appetite that reaches past a life's current borders toward what could still be true. Its gift is genuine largeness of spirit — optimism that is earned, generosity that costs something. Its shadow is expansion without limit: overreach, excess, a confidence so total it stops checking itself against the world. Tarnas's own historical correlations pair Jupiter …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, Jupiter is expansion, meaning, and faith — the search for truth and the capacity for growth, wisdom, and joy. Its light is generosity, optimism, and philosophical depth; its shadow, excess, overconfidence, and dogmatism. Jupiter's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Saturn

sections.Archetype: Saturn is necessity itself — structure, time, the limit that will not be argued with. It governs the reality principle: the discipline that turns a wish into a finished thing, the patience to stay with a difficulty long enough to actually learn from it. Its gift is mastery earned the slow way — competence, integrity, the kind of strength that only comes from having met a real limit and stayed. Its shadow is that same limit turned punitive: rigidity, fear, a harshness toward oneself or others mistaken for …
sections.See also: In the canonical Western reading, Saturn is structure, time, and responsibility — the relationship to limits, mastery, and the hard-won wisdom of endurance. Its light is discipline, integrity, and perseverance; its shadow, rigidity, fear, and control mistaken for standards. Saturn's fuller multi-voice reading — Ptolemy, Lilly, Jyotiṣa, Alan Leo, the planetary myths — lives in this library's other voice grammars, where every tradition answers for the same planet in its own terms.

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Saturn–Pluto

sections.The complex: When Saturn and Pluto meet, structure meets the underworld: the archetypal field Tarnas calls one of the most sobering in the astrological alphabet. Saturn is limit, consequence, the long discipline of what must be endured; Pluto is the elemental force beneath the floorboards — power, mortality, compulsion. Together they describe contraction: history's grimmest hours, when necessity closes in and nothing can be argued or wished away. This is not a punishing coincidence but a pattern, Tarnas argues, that recurs …
sections.In history: Tarnas correlates Saturn-Pluto alignments with three of the twentieth century's grimmest passages: the outbreak of the First World War (1914), the consolidation of totalitarian power leading into the Second World War (1939-41), and the September 11 attacks and the war on terror that followed (2001). In each, he reads the same signature — historical necessity closing down options, under conditions that felt, to those living through them, inescapable.
sections.A question: What in your life right now feels like necessity rather than choice — and what would it mean to meet it without either collapsing under it or pretending it isn't there?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Uranus–Pluto

sections.The complex: Uranus-Pluto is Tarnas's signature alignment — the pairing he treats as the deepest marker of epochal upheaval. Uranus supplies the sudden break, the individuating impulse that will not be governed; Pluto supplies the elemental force that makes the break irreversible. Together they read as revolution in the fullest sense: not reform but rupture, an eros unbound from whatever contained it — sexual, political, generational. Tarnas notes that this cycle moves slowly enough (Uranus and Pluto realign roughly once a …
sections.In history: Tarnas correlates the Uranus-Pluto conjunction of the 1960s (roughly 1960-1972) with the era's convergent upheavals — the civil rights movement, second-wave feminism, the sexual revolution, and the global wave of decolonization. He traces the prior conjunction to the revolutions of 1848 across Europe, and reads the Uranus-Pluto square of the 2010s (Occupy, the Arab Spring, and the decade's broader wave of populist and social-justice mobilization) as the same archetypal signature recurring in a different aspect.
sections.A question: Where in your own life is something asking to be broken open rather than managed — and can you tell the difference between destruction and a birth that requires it?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Jupiter–Uranus

sections.The complex: Jupiter is expansion and faith in possibility; Uranus is the sudden opening. Where they meet, Tarnas reads what he calls quantum leaps — moments when a door that seemed permanently shut simply isn't there anymore, and something that could not be reasoned into being arrives instead in a rush. This is the lighter cousin of Uranus-Pluto: less an epochal rupture than a burst, a widening, an invention or a liberation that expands what was previously thought possible. Its gift is exhilaration, discovery, the surprising …
sections.In history: Tarnas reads Jupiter-Uranus alignments as correlating with sudden expansions of freedom, knowledge, or opportunity — moments a society's sense of the possible widens quickly rather than gradually. He treats this cycle as recurring roughly every fourteen years, more frequent and more locally felt than the slower outer-planet alignments, which is why this grammar reads it with lower confidence than the Saturn-Pluto and Uranus-Pluto entries above — the book's own argument leans on the slower cycles for its central …
sections.A question: What became suddenly possible for you that you weren't expecting — and did you let yourself believe it, or wait for the catch?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Uranus–Neptune

sections.The complex: Uranus's sudden opening meets Neptune's dissolving of boundaries, and the result, Tarnas argues, is a distinctive cultural weather: visionary, idealistic, prone to utopian dreaming and genuine spiritual awakening at once. This is the complex behind a culture's romantic and mystical turns — moments when the given, literal world seems suddenly permeable, and both religious revival and psychedelic experiment become newly thinkable. Its light is real: awakening, inspiration, a collective loosening of what counted as …
sections.In history: Tarnas correlates the Uranus-Neptune conjunction of the early 1820s with the flowering of the Romantic movement in Europe — its visionary poetry, its reenchantment of nature, its revolt against Enlightenment rationalism. He reads the most recent conjunction, in the early 1990s, alongside the New Age movement's spread into the cultural mainstream and the sudden, hopeful, and often over-idealistic mood that followed the end of the Cold War.
sections.A question: Where has your imagination opened a door recently — and how would you know if what came through it was insight or wishful dreaming?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Saturn–Neptune

sections.The complex: Saturn's hard edge meets Neptune's dissolving tide, and something has to give. Tarnas reads this alignment as the archetypal signature of disillusionment — the moment a beautiful, inflated, or simply unexamined belief meets the ground and does not survive contact. This is the grief of the real: painful, but not without its own gift, because what Saturn-Neptune clears away was never as solid as it looked, and what remains afterward, though smaller, is at least true. At its best the complex is spiritual discipline …
sections.In history: Tarnas correlates the Saturn-Neptune conjunction of 1989 with the sudden, structural collapse of Soviet-bloc communism — an entire ideological edifice (Saturn) dissolving (Neptune) within months. He also reads the Saturn-Neptune opposition of 2006-07 alongside the unraveling of the speculative financial fantasies that produced the 2008 crash — a bubble (Neptune) meeting its reckoning (Saturn).
sections.A question: What belief of yours has quietly stopped being true — and can you let it go without deciding that nothing is left standing?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Saturn–Uranus

sections.The complex: Saturn conserves; Uranus breaks. Put in direct relationship, Tarnas reads this pairing as the archetypal tension of order against rupture — the argument, playing out in a single life or an entire society, between what has been built and earned versus what wants, urgently, to change. Neither side is simply right in this complex; Saturn without Uranus calcifies into rigidity, Uranus without Saturn dissipates into chaos that changes nothing durable. The complex's real question is whether the tension resolves into a …
sections.In history: Tarnas reads Saturn-Uranus oppositions and squares as correlating with periods of open ideological conflict between conserving and disrupting forces — he cites the tense years leading into the Second World War, when authoritarian order and revolutionary upheaval were in direct, unresolved contest across Europe, as one clear instance of the pattern. He treats the alignment as recurring roughly every twenty years, each time restaging the same argument in new material.
sections.A question: Where in your life are you defending a structure out of habit rather than conviction — or breaking one before you've actually tested whether it still serves you?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Jupiter–Saturn

sections.The complex: Jupiter and Saturn meet roughly every twenty years, in a cycle medieval and Renaissance astrologers called the Great Conjunction and treated as history's own metronome — the chronocrator, the timekeeper of ages. Tarnas revives this older tradition rather than inventing it: expansion (Jupiter) and structure (Saturn) in dialogue mark the intervals at which a society's operating assumptions get renegotiated, not always dramatically, but reliably. Every generation gets roughly one Jupiter-Saturn conjunction to define …
sections.In history: Tarnas draws directly on the older astrological tradition here: Kepler famously proposed the Star of Bethlehem was a Jupiter-Saturn conjunction (7 BCE), and medieval astrologers such as Māshā'allāh and Abū Ma'shar built entire theories of dynastic and religious change on the roughly 200-year shift of Great Conjunctions through the zodiac's elemental triplicities. Tarnas treats this historical astrological practice itself — not only the conjunctions — as evidence of how consistently different eras reached for the …
sections.A question: What social contract — a relationship, a job, a community's unwritten rules — are you due to renegotiate, whether or not anyone's called the moment yet?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Jupiter–Neptune

sections.The complex: Jupiter's expansiveness meets Neptune's dissolving of boundaries, and Tarnas reads the result as a complex of idealism running without a governor: faith, generosity, and genuine spiritual aspiration on one hand, inflation, credulity, and bubble-thinking on the other. This is the astrological signature of enthusiasm untethered from ground — a mood, individual or collective, in which belief outruns evidence and everyone involved feels, for a while, wonderful about it. The complex is not automatically negative …
sections.In history: Tarnas reads Jupiter-Neptune alignments as correlating with waves of religious revivalism and utopian social movements, and — in its more worldly register — with speculative financial exuberance: collective enthusiasm inflating an asset or an ideology well past what it can bear, before Saturn (in a later alignment) brings the accounting due. This grammar reads this cycle with lower confidence than the Saturn-Pluto and Uranus-Pluto entries above — Tarnas treats it as a secondary, faster-moving pattern rather than …
sections.A question: What are you currently more excited about than the evidence really supports — and is that a problem, or is the excitement itself doing something useful?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Jupiter–Pluto

sections.The complex: Jupiter's expansive reach meets Pluto's elemental force, and Tarnas reads the combination as magnified will — ambition given both scope and depth at once. This is the complex behind empire, in the literal and the personal sense: the drive not merely to grow but to consolidate power over what has grown. Its gift is the capacity to enact a vision at real scale; its danger is that the same scale makes the abuse of power correspondingly larger. Jupiter-Pluto rarely produces small gestures — whatever it touches, it …
sections.In history: Tarnas correlates Jupiter-Pluto alignments with periods of dramatic expansion of political or economic power — he reads the mid-1930s conjunction alongside the rapid, expansionist consolidation of Nazi Germany's ambitions in that period as one instance of the pattern: expansive will (Jupiter) fused with an unignorable underworld force (Pluto).
sections.A question: Where in your life has your ambition grown bigger than your willingness to be honest about its cost?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Neptune–Pluto

sections.The complex: Neptune and Pluto move so slowly relative to each other — a single alignment lasts centuries — that Tarnas treats their cycle not as a marker of events but as the deep background hum beneath an entire age: the shared, largely unconscious myth a civilization is living inside without quite noticing it has one. Neptune dissolves and re-enchants; Pluto works underground, in slow transformation rather than sudden event. Together, across a span longer than any single life, they describe the kind of change a culture only …
sections.In history: Tarnas treats the Renaissance-through-Enlightenment transition — the multi-century shift from the medieval to the modern Western worldview he chronicled in his earlier book The Passion of the Western Mind — as unfolding under the most recent long Neptune-Pluto alignment. Because Pluto was not discovered until 1930 and Neptune until 1846, no observer at the time could have named the correlation; Tarnas's reading here is necessarily retrospective and long-range, and this grammar holds it that way — as the least …
sections.A question: What quiet assumption is your whole generation living inside, that a much later century might name as clearly as we now name the Middle Ages?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Sun–Saturn

sections.The complex: The Sun is the will to be someone in particular; Saturn is the limit that will inevitably meets — time, mortality, the slow discipline of building something durable. Read together, Tarnas's archetypal framework treats Sun-Saturn as the complex of earned identity: selfhood that has been tested against real constraint rather than simply asserted. Its gift, when the tension is worked rather than avoided, is authority that has actually been paid for — competence, mastery, a self that can bear weight. Its shadow is an …
sections.In history: Sun-Saturn falls outside Cosmos and Psyche's own historical case studies, which track slower outer-planet-to-outer-planet alignments across collective history — this pairing's cycle (roughly annual) is far too fast to mark an epoch the way the book's central alignments do. This reading instead extends Tarnas's archetypal vocabulary — the Sun as core identity, Saturn as structure and limit — to the personal register, offered honestly as this grammar's own interpretation, not as a claim from the book's own data.
sections.A question: What have you built that actually cost you something — and does it feel more like a cage or a foundation?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Sun–Pluto

sections.The complex: The Sun's will to shine meets Pluto's elemental undertow, and the complex that results is intensity: identity forged not gently but through confrontation with what is compulsive, mortal, or hidden in oneself. This is the astrological signature of the phoenix rather than the steady climb — a self that has gone down into something and come back changed, sometimes unrecognizably. Its gift is depth and a kind of hard-won authenticity that cannot be faked; its risk is a will to power that mistakes domination for …
sections.In history: Sun-Pluto falls outside Cosmos and Psyche's own historical case studies, which track slower outer-planet-to-outer-planet alignments across collective history — this pairing's cycle (roughly annual) is far too fast to mark an epoch the way the book's central alignments do. This reading instead extends Tarnas's archetypal vocabulary — the Sun as core identity, Pluto as the underworld drive — to the personal register, offered honestly as this grammar's own interpretation, not as a claim from the book's own data.
sections.A question: What part of yourself did you have to go into the dark to actually find?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Venus–Mars

sections.The complex: Venus and Mars are the oldest planetary pair astrology has read as a couple — attraction and drive, the desire to harmonize and the desire to act. Where they meet, the complex Tarnas's framework describes is eros in the fullest sense: not romance alone but the whole current that makes a person move toward what they want, tempered or untempered by the wish to also be in right relationship with it. At its best this pairing is passionate cooperation — desire that knows how to ask, not only take. At its worst it is …
sections.In history: Venus-Mars falls outside Cosmos and Psyche's own historical case studies, which track slower outer-planet-to-outer-planet alignments across collective history — this pairing's cycle (roughly two years) is far too fast to mark an epoch the way the book's central alignments do. This reading instead extends Tarnas's archetypal vocabulary — Venus as the value-and-harmony principle, Mars as the drive-and-assertion principle — to the personal register, offered honestly as this grammar's own interpretation, not as a …
sections.A question: In your closest relationship right now, which is more often missing — the wanting, or the willingness to ask for it directly?

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Moon–Saturn

sections.The complex: The Moon is the tide of feeling — need, memory, the instinctive reach for comfort; Saturn is the boundary that says not yet, or not like that. Together they describe the complex of emotional discipline: a nervous system that has learned, sometimes the hard way, to hold feeling inside a structure rather than be swept by it. Done well this produces real emotional maturity — steadiness that is not the same as numbness. Done poorly it produces a wall where warmth should be: feeling so thoroughly governed that it stops …

This reading instead extends Tarnas's archetypal vocabulary — the Moon as feeling and instinct, Saturn as structure and limit — to the personal register, offered honestly as this grammar's own interpretation, not as a claim from the book's …

passages.grammar_name: Archetypal Astrology — planetary pairs, after Tarnas
passages.name: Mercury–Uranus

sections.The complex: Mercury is the mind in its ordinary motion — noticing, naming, connecting; Uranus is the mind interrupted by something it did not see coming. Together this complex describes the sudden thought: insight that arrives whole, unannounced, sometimes disruptive to whatever the mind had settled into believing five minutes earlier. Its gift is genuine originality — the kind of idea that could not have been reasoned into existence step by step. Its shadow is a mind so addicted to the jolt of the new that it can't stay with …
sections.In history: Mercury-Uranus falls outside Cosmos and Psyche's own historical case studies, which track slower outer-planet-to-outer-planet alignments across collective history — this pairing's cycle (about eighteen months) is far too fast to mark an epoch the way the book's central alignments do. This reading instead extends Tarnas's archetypal vocabulary — Mercury as mind and communication, Uranus as sudden awakening — to the personal register, offered honestly as this grammar's own interpretation, not as a claim from the …

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Conjunction

sections.Canonical: Fusion. Two principles occupy one point and act as a single, intensified force — the strongest of all configurations, neutral in itself: it amplifies whatever it joins. Light: concentrated power, unified purpose. Shadow: the blind spot of energies you can no longer see apart.

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Sextile

sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos): [Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos I, c. 150 CE · Ashmand tr. 1822] "In all parts at the hexagonal distance from each other, containing between them two-thirds of a right angle, or two signs, or sixty degrees." "The sextile is called harmonious, because it is constituted between signs of the same kind" — "being formed between either all feminine or all masculine signs." Harmony, for Ptolemy, is a fact of geometry and gender-of-sign, not of feeling. (Verbatim Ashmand, verified in grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand; confidence: high.)

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Sextile

sections.Lilly (1647): [William Lilly, Christian Astrology, 1647] The sextile and trine "are arguments of Love, Unity and Friendship" — the sextile the milder of the two, the trine "more forcible." In Lilly's horary practice significators in sextile promise the matter may be brought to pass, though with some endeavour — a friendship that must still be acted on. (The quoted phrases are corroborated this session via a single secondary reproduction of the tradition's aspect doctrine, renaissanceastrology.com's Ptolemaic-aspects page …

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Sextile

sections.Canonical: Opportunity. Sixty degrees apart, in compatible elements — a door held open that still asks you to walk through it. Light: cooperation, communication between energies, easy exchange. Shadow: talents left idle because nothing forces them; the missed opening.

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Square

sections.Ptolemy (Tetrabiblos): [Ptolemy, Tetrabiblos I, c. 150 CE · Ashmand tr. 1822] "In all parts at the quadrate distance from each other, containing between them exactly one right angle, or three signs, or ninety degrees." "The opposition and quartile are considered to be discordant" — "because they are configurations made between signs not of the same kind, but of different natures and sexes." Discord, again, is structural: signs a square apart never share element or gender. (Verbatim Ashmand, verified in grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand …

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Square

sections.Lilly (1647): [William Lilly, Christian Astrology, 1647] The quartile is "an aspect of imperfect enmity" — enmity, but not past mending: Lilly's horary tradition reads significators in square as a matter that may yet be effected, but only with labour, difficulty, and interruption, where the trine would have carried it easily. (The quoted phrase is corroborated this session via a single secondary reproduction, renaissanceastrology.com's Ptolemaic-aspects page; confidence: ○. The horary gloss is paraphrase.)

passages.grammar_name: The Aspects, Commented — Ptolemy · Lilly · Canonical
passages.name: Square

sections.Canonical: Friction that builds. Ninety degrees — two drives at cross purposes, neither able to ignore the other. The square is where the work of a life tends to concentrate. Light: motivation, breakthrough, strength earned through challenge. Shadow: chronic conflict re-enacted instead of worked.

"The trine is called harmonious, because it is constituted between signs of the same kind" — signs a trine apart share their element, the deepest sameness Ptolemy's scheme recognizes. passages.name: Cardinal Cross

sections.What it is: The school groups the four cardinal signs as a cross and ties it to beginnings of the largest kind; the crisis it names for this cross is initiation. Other schools call the same four signs the cardinal modality. Signs: Aries, Cancer, Libra, Capricorn.
sections.How the school uses it (the record): The book ties each cross to a stage on its path, from ordinary experience (Mutable) through discipleship (Fixed) to initiation (Cardinal), and says the arms of the crosses will one day matter more than the houses in the soul's chart. This library gives that as the school's own teaching, never as a measure of anyone. Most charts have planets on more than one cross.
sections.An invitation: Where in your life does something new keep wanting to begin?

passages.grammar_name: Esoteric Astrology — the Bailey school, paraphrased
passages.name: Vulcan (hypothetical)

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): Vulcan rules Taurus in the esoteric and the hierarchical columns. The book pictures it as a smith at the forge, working in the densest material, going down into the depths to shape something useful and beautiful: an energy that starts things and also breaks old forms. It links Vulcan closely with the Sun, sometimes hidden behind it, sometimes standing for it.
sections.In the sky: No such planet has been found. In 1859 the astronomer Urbain Le Verrier proposed a planet inside Mercury's orbit to explain an unexplained drift in Mercury's path. Claimed sightings were never confirmed, and general relativity (1915) explained the drift without it. Vulcan is a symbol with no position.
sections.How to look through it here: As a ruler only. Readers of this school sometimes look at Vulcan through the Sun (the link above) or through the Moon (another passage of the book). Some software offers a 20th-century hypothetical ephemeris for it; that is a guess, not an observation, and this library does not use it.
sections.An invitation: What in you works slowly out of sight, shaping something that is not ready to be seen yet?

passages.name: The Earth (as a ruler)

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): The Earth rules Sagittarius in the esoteric column and Gemini in the hierarchical one. The book counts it among the planets it does not call sacred. Few other schools give the Earth a sign at all.
sections.In the sky: Real, and underfoot. A chart is drawn from the Earth, so the Earth has no place of its own on it; practitioners who use it put it exactly opposite the Sun. That is a convention, not an observation.
sections.An invitation: If the ground you stand on had something to say about where you are aiming, what would it say?

sections.In this school (our paraphrase): Most modern astrology gives Pluto to Scorpio. In this school's table Pluto rules Pisces, in the esoteric and the hierarchical columns, and Scorpio keeps Mars. The book is not consistent about it: another passage gives Pluto to Scorpio and calls Mars Pluto's other self.
sections.Reading it: Many schools read Pluto as endings and renewal. Set beside Pisces, the last sign of the wheel, this could mean the close of a cycle. It could also mean a sensitivity that has been through something and come out changed. What does it mean to you?
sections.An invitation: What is ending for you, and what might it be clearing room for?

sections.In the text: Chapter II of the Bṛhat Jātaka ("Definitions and Elementary Planetary Principles") gives the Sun a place among the Kālapuruṣa correspondences — the scheme that maps the nine grahas onto the body and rank of a cosmic "Time-Person": the Sun and Moon are its kings, and the Sun and Moon together are called the "kings" of the planetary hierarchy, with Mars as general, Mercury as first prince, Jupiter and Venus as counsellors, and Saturn as servant. The Sun is said to be strong in bones and to preside over copper …
sections.What this lens reads: In tropical astrology the Sun anchors the whole zodiac (0° Aries is defined by the Sun's position at the equinox); in Jyotiṣa the Sun is one king among grahas measured against the fixed stars, roughly 24° behind its tropical degree today. Same star, two honest coordinate systems — the gap between them is the thing worth noticing, not a discrepancy to resolve.
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. Iyer (188: Chapter II (‘Definitions and Elementary Principles — Planetary’), stanza 1: ‘To the Kalapurusha, the Sun is the soul… Of the planets the Sun and Moon are kings, Mars is General, Mercury is the first prince, Jupiter and Venus are counsellors and Saturn is servant.’ Stanzas 4–5 give his colour and rulership: ‘The Sun is of a red and dark-brown color… The Sun presides over copper color… The Sun is Agni [the fire-god]… The Sun presides over east.’ Stanza 7 places him by caste and temperament: ‘Mars and the Sun are …

sections.In the text: Chapter II describes the Moon-native's body as "well rounded," full of wind and phlegm, intelligent, and of sweet speech; white is the colour Candra presides over. In the Kālapuruṣa scheme the Moon is mind (manas) and, with the Sun, one of the two "kings" among the grahas. (Paraphrase with short quoted phrases from Chapter II via the chestofbooks.com mirror of the 1885 Chidambaram Iyer translation; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: Where the tropical Western literature (see grammars/western-astrology-canonical, grammars/alan-leo) reads the Moon as feeling and instinct, this text reads it as manas — mind itself, the faculty that receives and processes, not merely emotion. The Sanskrit vocabulary carves the psyche differently than the Greek-derived one does; that's a real difference in what a chart is claimed to show, not just a translation gap.
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. sections.In the text: Chapter II assigns Mars (Kuja, also Aṅgāraka — "the red-hot one/coal-man") blood-red as his colour, consistent across the classical Sanskrit tradition (rakta varṇa, "blood-coloured"). In the Kālapuruṣa scheme Mars is bala, strength — the general among the grahas, ranked directly under the two royal luminaries. (Paraphrase; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: Mars-as-general is a specific, martial-bureaucratic image — a planetary hierarchy modeled on a royal court, not a modern psychological 'drive.' Worth sitting with before assuming every tradition's Mars means the same private thing it means in a Sun-sign column.

sections.In the text: Chapter II lists several names for Jupiter — Jīva, Aṅgirā, Suraguru, Vācaspati, Ijya — and describes him as corpulent in body, with golden locks and eyes, of moral character, and phlegmatic. In the Kālapuruṣa scheme Jupiter (with Venus) is a counsellor, and separately Jupiter is named as knowledge and health. (Paraphrase with quoted phrases via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)

Two traditions independently landing on 'the wise, generous, expansive one' for the same slow bright planet is worth noticing without over-claiming why.

Notably, in the received Sanskrit tradition Śukra is also a masculine figure (sage/preceptor of the asuras) — a reminder that 'Venus' the Roman name and Śukra the Sanskrit graha are not …

sections.In the text: Chapter II gives Saturn several names — Kona, Manda ("the slow one"), Sūryaputra ("son of the Sun"), Asita ("the black one") — and describes him as lazy, with eyes of a golden colour, a thin and tall body, large teeth, stiff hair, and a windy constitution; black is his colour. In the Kālapuruṣa scheme Saturn is named as śoka, sorrow, and holds the rank of servant — the lowest of the nine. (Paraphrase with quoted phrases via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)

'Sūryaputra,' son of the Sun, also ties Śani into a specific mythological genealogy this grammar doesn't unpack further; see the Vedic-myth cross-references in grammars/planetary-myths.

Stanza 2 names him: ‘Kona, Manda, Suryaputra (son of the Sun) and Asita (the black planet) are the names of Saturn.’ Stanzas 4–5: ‘Saturn is black… Saturn over black color… Saturn is Brahma… Saturn [presides over] west.’ Stanza 6: ‘Mercury and Saturn are hermaphrodite planets’ — glossed as the male hermaphrodite — and ‘Saturn is air.’ Stanza 7: ‘Saturn is a Chandala [an outcaste]… Mars and Saturn …

sections.In the text: Rāhu is one of the two chāyā grahas ("shadow planets") of Jyotiṣa — not a physical body but the Moon's ascending node, the point where the Moon's path crosses the Sun's. Sanskrit names recorded for Rāhu include Tamas ("darkness"), Agu, and Asura; the mythic frame is the severed head of an asura who drank a portion of the gods' amṛta (nectar of immortality) and was decapitated by Viṣṇu for the theft, the head living on to periodically swallow the Sun or Moon — the tradition's own account of eclipses. Held at low …
sections.What this lens reads: The nodes have no Western planetary counterpart at all in the tropical tradition this site otherwise carries — they are Jyotiṣa's own invention for handling eclipses astrologically, and a place where this lens genuinely adds a category the others don't have, rather than just relabeling a shared planet.
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. Iyer (188: Chapter II, stanza 3, gives the only naming stanza this translation devotes to the lunar nodes: ‘Tama (darkness), Agu and Asura are the names of Rahu (the Moon’s ascending node); Sikhi is the name of Ketu (the Moon’s descending node).’ That is the whole of the direct textual material on Rāhu in Chidambaram Iyer’s Chapter II — the translator moves from Jupiter and Venus’s names in stanza 3 straight to the seven visible planets’ colours in stanza 4, without giving Rāhu a body-and-temperament stanza the way he does …

sections.In the text: Ketu is the second chāyā graha, the descending node — the same severed-asura body from the waist down, in the eclipse myth that pairs with Rāhu (see graha-rahu). One recorded name is Śikhin ("the crested/flagged one," evoking a comet's tail). As with Rāhu, this session's search found the mythic and nomenclature material solidly but did not locate a specific graha-description passage from Chapter II of the Chidambaram Iyer translation naming Ketu directly — flagged honestly rather than invented (confidence: ◆).
sections.What this lens reads: Rāhu and Ketu, always exactly opposite each other in the sky, read together as one severed body split by a boundary — a vivid, non-Western way of representing that eclipses are structurally paired (a lunar eclipse near one node, a solar eclipse near the same node roughly two weeks later).
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. Iyer (188: Chapter II, stanza 3, names Ketu in the same single line that names Rāhu: ‘Tama (darkness), Agu and Asura are the names of Rahu (the Moon’s ascending node); Sikhi is the name of Ketu (the Moon’s descending node).’ ‘Sikhi’ — the crested or flame-bannered one — is the only name Chidambaram Iyer’s translation gives Ketu in this chapter; unlike the seven visible grahas, Ketu receives no colour, caste, temperament, or bodily-strength stanza here.
