sections.In the text: Chapter I ("Definitions and Elementary Zodiacal Principles") of the Bṛhat Jātaka gives Meṣa the colour red, classes it among the quadruped (catuṣpada) signs, and — as a movable (cara) sign along with Karka, Tulā, and Makara — associates its trigon (with Siṃha and Dhanu) with the eastern direction. It is counted among the signs said to rise "with their feet." (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: The classificatory apparatus here — quadruped/biped/aquatic, movable/fixed/common, directional trigons — runs strikingly parallel to Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos (compare grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand's Aries), right down to shared categories like 'quadruped.' Whether that is convergent technical reasoning about the same visible zodiac or a trace of the historical transmission the Jyotiṣa dossier flags as contested (research/views/jyotisha.md) is an open question this grammar doesn't resolve.

Unusually, Mithuna is noted as an exception among the otherwise "night"-rising signs. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: "Mithuna" means a pair/couple in Sanskrit — the same twin-image the Greek Dídymoi (Gemini) carries, on an unrelated etymology. Two traditions independently seeing a pair of figures in the same patch of sky is a small, concrete instance of humans converging on similar readings from the actual star pattern (Castor and Pollux), not from shared doctrine.

sections.What this lens reads: An aquatic, movable, northern-trigon sign for the Moon's own house lines up with the tropical Cancer's watery, lunar, cardinal reading (compare grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand) — again, shared structural logic rather than shared doctrine.

sections.What this lens reads: "Kanyā" — maiden — is a direct semantic cousin of the Greco-Roman Virgo (also "maiden"/"virgin"), on the same unrelated-etymology logic as Mithuna/Gemini above: different words, same figure read into roughly the same stretch of sky.

sections.In the text: Chapter I gives Tulā a black colour, classes it among the biped signs, the movable signs (with Meṣa, Karka, Makara), and shares Mithuna and Kumbha's western-trigon association. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: "Tulā" means balance/scale in Sanskrit — the same image as the Greco-Roman Libra, the one zodiac sign in both traditions represented by an object rather than a person or animal. Whether this is a shared inheritance or an independent invention (both cultures having scales as a common tool) is exactly the kind of question the transmission dossier (research/views/jyotisha.md) holds open rather than settles.

sections.In the text: Chapter I gives Vṛścika a gold colour and, notably, marks it as the only centipede (śatapada, "hundred-footed") sign in the whole zodiac — a distinct classificatory category from quadruped, biped, or aquatic. It is a fixed sign, sharing the northern-trigon association with Karka and Mīna. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: A scorpion needs its own animal category ("hundred-footed") that no other sign shares — a small, concrete example of how far this classification scheme's own internal logic diverges from a simple biped/quadruped split, on a sign both traditions independently image as a scorpion or stinging creature.
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. sections.In the text: Chapter I gives Dhanu the colour of paddy husk and treats it as a split sign: its second half is classed quadruped, its first half biped — a half-and-half classification shared with Makara (split the other way). It is a common/dual sign, sharing the eastern-trigon association with Meṣa and Siṃha. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: "Dhanu" means bow — an archer, same as the Greco-Roman Sagittarius's centaur-archer, and the same half-human/half-animal duality shows up independently in the sign's own classification scheme (half biped, half quadruped) as well as in its symbol. A striking convergence, held here as fact-plus-question, not proof of either shared or separate origin.

sections.In the text: Chapter I gives Makara a white-red colour and, like Dhanu, splits its classification: the first half aquatic, matching Karka and Mīna, the second half quadruped, matching Meṣa, Vṛṣabha, and Siṃha. It is a movable sign, sharing the southern-trigon association with Vṛṣabha and Kanyā. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: Makara is imaged as a crocodile-fish hybrid (the traditional makara creature) — and, tellingly, its own textual classification splits it half-aquatic, half-land, mirroring the hybrid symbol in the technical scheme itself rather than only in the artwork. Compare the Western sea-goat image for Capricorn (grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand): two traditions, two different hybrid sea-creatures, same zodiac position.
sections.The record — Varāhamihira, tr. sections.In the text: Chapter I gives Kumbha the colour of a mongoose and classes it among the biped signs and the fixed signs, sharing the western-trigon association with Mithuna and Tulā. (Paraphrase with quoted classificatory terms via chestofbooks.com; confidence: ○.)
sections.What this lens reads: "Kumbha" means water-pot — the water-bearer image, close kin to the Greco-Roman Aquarius's water-carrier, yet classed here as a biped (human-form) sign rather than an aquatic one: the vessel is watery, the bearer is not, a small but real reminder that these classification schemes track the sign's imagined body, not its symbolic association.

sections.What this lens reads: "Mīna" simply means fish — the plainest possible name for the same paired-fish image the Greco-Roman Pisces carries. The final sign in both traditions' twelve-fold wheel, closing the same circle by two independently-arrived-at routes.

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Sin (the Moon)

sections.The omen: "When the Moon disappears, evil will befall the land. When the Moon disappears out of its reckoning, an eclipse will take place." A companion report reads: "When the Moon reaches the Sun and with it fades out of sight, its horns being dim, there will be truth in the land, and the son will speak the truth with his father." (Quoted from R. Campbell Thompson, The Reports of the Magicians and Astrologers of Nineveh and Babylon, Vol. II, London, 1900 — a public-domain edition of Neo-Assyrian scholars' letters to the …
sections.Who this power was: Sin (Sumerian Nanna) is one of Mesopotamia's oldest attested gods, worshipped from at least c. 3500 BCE as moon-god and a god of wisdom, seated at his great ziggurat in Ur; by the Ur III period he was also cast as judge of the dead. See grammars/planetary-myths for the fuller myth-history of Sin/Nanna alongside the Greco-Roman and Vedic Moon figures.
sections.What this lens reads: The Moon's own irregular disappearance and reappearance (its monthly phases, and especially an unscheduled early or late vanishing that signals an eclipse) is read directly as omen material — a system built entirely around watching what the sky visibly does, with no birth chart, no zodiac signs yet, and no claim on any one person's fate.

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Šamaš (the Sun)

sections.The omen: "If the Moon and Sun are visible [together], the king of the land will be wise." The scholars' commentary on this report explains the timing: on the 14th day of the month, when 'god is seen with god' (Moon with Sun, i.e. a mid-month conjunction-adjacent visibility), the omen is read as favourable for the king's judgment. (Quoted/paraphrased from R. Campbell Thompson's 1900 edition of the Nineveh scholars' reports, per secondary reproduction; confidence: ○.)
sections.Who this power was: Šamaš (Sumerian Utu) was sun-god and god of justice, believed to see every human act from his daily chariot-ride across the sky — Hammurabi's law code claims Šamaš as the source of its justice. With Sin (Moon) and Ištar (Venus) he formed an astral triad governing the Babylonian omen-sky. See grammars/planetary-myths for the fuller myth-history.
sections.What this lens reads: Justice and truthful judgment are read directly off a Sun-Moon visibility pattern — the sun-god who 'sees every human act' is, fittingly, the power invoked when the omen concerns whether the king himself will judge rightly. The moral content of the deity and the content of the omen are the same idea, twice.

passages.name: Ištar (Venus)

sections.The omen: The great Venus omen series — Tablet 63 of Enūma Anu Enlil, known as "the Venus Tablet of Ammiṣaduqa," preserved in later copies and first published in a full public-domain translation by Stephen Langdon and J. K. Fotheringham (The Venus Tablets of Ammizaduga, Oxford University Press, 1928) — records Venus's dates of first and last visibility as morning and evening star across a 21-year cycle, reading omens from each appearance and disappearance for the king and the land. Morris Jastrow (1898) records the …
sections.Who this power was: Ištar's own Akkadian planetary name was Dilbat, "the Announcer" — also the name of a Babylonian city, likely her cult seat under this planetary form. See grammars/planetary-myths for Ištar/Inanna's fuller myth-history across traditions.
sections.What this lens reads: Venus is the one planet whose two faces — morning star and evening star — are visibly different phenomena to a naked-eye observer (it disappears into the Sun's glare and reappears on the other side), and this omen tradition builds an entire calendar and its own goddess-title ('the Announcer') around exactly that visible duality, centuries before anyone could explain it as one planet's orbit.

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Nergal (Mars)

sections.The omen: "When Mars stands opposite a planet, corn will be valuable." "When Mars approaches the Moon and stands [there], the Moon will cause evil to inhabit the land." "When Mars approaches Scorpio, the prince will die by a scorpion's sting, and his son after him will take the throne." (Quoted from R. Campbell Thompson, The Reports of the Magicians and Astrologers of Nineveh and Babylon, Vol. II (1900), public domain; confidence: ○ — corroborated across multiple secondary reproductions this session.)
sections.Who this power was: Nergal, Mars's Mesopotamian identification, was a god of war, plague, and the underworld — consort of Ereshkigal, ruler of the land of the dead. His association with the fiercest and most unpredictable of the visible wandering stars follows directly from that portfolio.
sections.What this lens reads: Mars-approaches-Scorpio-and-the-prince-dies is a strikingly literal reading: the sting-bearing constellation and a violent, unlucky planet, read together as a stinging death. This is omen logic at its most image-driven — the sky's shapes are read almost like a rebus, not abstracted into a general 'malefic' principle the way Ptolemy later does (compare grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand's Mars).

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Marduk (Jupiter)

sections.The omen: "When Jupiter passes to the place of sunset, there will be dwelling securely; kindly peace will descend on the land." "When Jupiter assumes a brilliance in the tropic of Cancer and becomes Nibiru, Akkad will overflow with plenty, the king of Akkad will grow powerful." "When a halo surrounds the Moon and Jupiter stands within it, the king of Akkad will be besieged." The reports name Jupiter's phases as separate divine identities: 'Marduk is Umun-pa-uddu at its appearance; when it has risen for two hours it becomes …
sections.Who this power was: Marduk was Babylon's own patron god, head of the pantheon by the Old Babylonian period and hero of the creation epic Enūma Eliš; his identification with the brightest wandering star after Venus follows his supreme rank.
sections.What this lens reads: Naming Jupiter's stations (rising, culmination) as distinct divine names (Sagmigar, Nibiru) shows the omen tradition wasn't reading one fixed 'Jupiter'; it was reading a sequence of appearances, each a different manifestation to be watched separately — a far more granular sky-reading practice than the single-fixed-planet-meaning model later traditions (Hellenistic, Jyotiṣa, Renaissance) largely settle into.

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Ninurta (Saturn)

sections.The omen: This item is honestly thinner than its six companions. This session located Saturn's Akkadian planetary name, Kayamānu ("the steady/constant one"), and secondary scholarship noting that some omen-series glosses actually equate Saturn's path with 'the path of the Sun' — Saturn was sometimes treated in this tradition as a kind of nocturnal counterpart or double of the Sun rather than folded cleanly into a single fixed god-identification. A specific quoted protasis-apodosis omen line naming Ninurta and Saturn …
sections.Who this power was: Ninurta was a Sumerian warrior and farmer-god, associated with the plough, the hunt, and (in some but not all reconstructions) with Saturn's identification among the classical seven — the planetary attributions in this system are not uniformly agreed across tablets, periods, or modern scholars, and this grammar does not paper over that.
sections.What this lens reads: Not every ancient planet-god mapping is as clean or as well-attested as Mars=Nergal or Venus=Ištar; Saturn's identification is comparatively under-documented in the sources this session could reach. An honest gap — flagged rather than filled with invented content — is itself informative about how uneven the surviving record is, five thousand years on.

passages.grammar_name: Mesopotamian Omen-Craft — The Seven Watched Powers
passages.name: Nabû (Mercury)

sections.The omen: As with Ninurta, this item is honestly thin on omen-specific material. Mercury moves too fast and stays too close to the Sun to have generated the same volume of surviving omen reports as the five slower, more easily tracked classical planets — this session did not locate a specific quoted Mercury/Nabû omen line from Thompson's 1900 reports or another PD source. What is well documented is Nabû's mythological and cultic profile: patron of scribes, writing, and wisdom, son of Marduk, rising to near-equal rank with …
sections.Who this power was: Nabû, patron of scribes and writing, is Mercury's Mesopotamian identification — the same fast, close-to-the-Sun planet the Greco-Roman Hermes/Mercury and the Vedic Budha also single out for communication and cleverness (see grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand and grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka).
sections.What this lens reads: Three unrelated traditions — Babylonian, Greco-Roman, Vedic — independently attach a writing/speech/cleverness portfolio to the same fast, hard-to-see planet. That convergence is worth noting on its own; it is not, on the evidence this session could gather, backed by a Mesopotamian omen-report quotation the way Mars, Venus, Jupiter, the Sun, and the Moon are here — an honest asymmetry in what survives, not a claim that Mercury omens didn't exist.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Sun

sections.Greco-Roman: Helios, a Titan, drove a four-horse chariot across the sky each day, lighting the world from dawn to dusk. By the Hellenistic period the Olympian Apollo — god of prophecy, music, and healing — had absorbed most of Helios's solar identity in cult and art, though the two were never formally merged in myth. Sources: Wikipedia, "Selene" (cross-referenced) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selene; Greek Names, "Greek names of the planets" — https://www.greek-names.info/greek-names-of-the-planets/ (confidence: ○ — …
sections.Vedic (graha): Sūrya is the graha of soul, vitality, and self-worth — Jyotiṣa treats him as king among the nine grahas and the significator (kāraka) of ego, father, and life-force. He rides a seven-horse chariot driven by Aruṇa, the horses named for the seven Vedic poetic meters (chandas); his arrival is heralded by the dawn-goddess Uṣas. The Ṛgveda's Gāyatrī mantra (3.62.10) is addressed to Sūrya-as-Savitṛ. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — see Wikipedia, "Surya" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surya; Budaya Bali, "God Surya …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Shamash (Sumerian Utu) was sun-god and god of justice — riding his chariot by day, he was believed to see every human act and so judge right from wrong; Hammurabi's law code claims Shamash as its source. With Sin (Moon) and Ishtar (Venus) he formed an astral triad governing the Babylonian omen-sky, the oldest documented layer beneath the later Greco-Roman planet names. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Utu-Shamash" — https://www.worldhistory.org/Utu-Shamash/; Britannica, "Shamash" — …
sections.What the lens reads: Three unrelated cultures pointed at the same bright disk and each built a different story: a chariot-driving Titan who became a healer-god, a soul-significator riding meters-of-poetry horses, a judge who sees every human act. None of this is a claim that the Sun causes anything — it is a record of how differently situated humans, looking at the same sky, made sense together. The disagreement between the three readings IS the content.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Moon

sections.Greco-Roman: Selene, a Titan daughter of Hyperion and Theia, drove her own moon-chariot nightly across the sky, sister to the sun-god Helios; the Romans called her Luna, who had a temple on Rome's Aventine Hill. In post-classical practice Selene/Luna increasingly blended with Artemis/Diana, goddess of the hunt and wilderness, even though the two began as separate figures — one purely a sky-orb goddess, the other a broader nature deity. Sources: Wikipedia, "Selene" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selene; Theoi Project, "Selene" …
sections.Vedic (graha): Chandra (also called Soma, "the bright drop") governs the mind (manas) in Jyotiṣa — a fast-moving, changeable graha tied to emotion, memory, and the 27 nakṣatras, mythologized as his 27 wives, daughters of Daksha. Chandra's favoritism toward Rohiṇī drew Daksha's curse of a wasting sickness, later softened into the Moon's waxing-and-waning cycle — the tradition's own explanation for lunar phases. Whether "Soma" originally meant the Moon versus the ritual drink varies by textual layer, sources note. As taught in …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Nanna (Akkadian Sin), one of Mesopotamia's oldest attested gods (from c. 3500 BCE), was worshipped as moon-god and god of wisdom at his great ziggurat in Ur; during the Ur III period he was additionally cast as judge of the dead. Son of Enlil and Ninlil, he was symbolized by the crescent moon. Source: World History Encyclopedia, "Nanna" — https://www.worldhistory.org/Nanna/ (confidence: ○ — single strong tertiary source, content consistent with other reference summaries).
sections.What the lens reads: A Titan sister on a nightly chariot ride, a wisdom-god whose crescent watches from a ziggurat in Ur, a changeable mind-graha with 27 star-brides — three cultures, one visibly-changing light in the night sky. Nobody in this grammar is claiming the Moon governs mood; the claim is narrower and more honest: humans across millennia independently reached for story to hold what they could plainly see changing shape above them.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Mercury

sections.Greco-Roman: Hermes, son of Zeus and the nymph Maia, served as herald and messenger of the Olympian gods and patron of travelers, merchants, orators, and — frankly — thieves, a boundary-crosser by nature. Rome adopted him as Mercury by the 4th century BCE, merging him with the Etruscan Turms; the name likely derives from merx, "merchandise." Mercury kept Hermes's winged sandals, winged cap, and caduceus. Sources: Wikipedia, "Hermes" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermes; Britannica, "Mercury" — …
sections.Vedic (graha): Budha (not to be confused with the Buddha) personifies buddhi, intellect — Jyotiṣa's significator of communication, learning, and adaptable thinking, said to take on the qualities of whichever planet it conjoins. His origin myth is unusually charged: born of Chandra's (the Moon's) affair with Tārā, wife of Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), a lineage dispute called the Tārakāmaya war. Budha later married Ilā and fathered Purūravas, founder of the lunar dynasty. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Budha" — …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Nabu, patron of scribes, writing, and wisdom, rose to prominence in the 1st millennium BCE as the son of Marduk of Babylon; each New Year his statue traveled from his own city, Borsippa, to pay respects to his father, and by the Neo-Babylonian period he stood nearly equal to Marduk as co-ruler of the pantheon. His signature task was inscribing the Tablet of Destinies. Sources: Ancient Origins, "Nabu" — https://www.ancient-origins.net/myths-legends-africa/nabu-0014933; Wikipedia, "Nabu" — …
sections.What the lens reads: A trickster-herald who invented commerce, an intellect-graha born of a scandalous lunar affair, a divine scribe who wrote the world's fate on a tablet — three very different plots converge on the same idea: this fast, changeable point of light governs thinking, language, and the crossing of boundaries. That convergence is interesting; it is not evidence any of the three literally happened.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Venus

sections.Greco-Roman: Aphrodite's birth has two competing accounts even within Greek sources: Hesiod's Theogony has her rising from sea-foam formed when Cronus cast Uranus's severed body into the water; Homer's Iliad instead calls her daughter of Zeus and Dione. Rome's Venus began as a goddess of gardens and spring growth before being formally identified with Aphrodite around the 3rd century BCE, per the historian Livy, after which she absorbed Aphrodite's love-and-beauty portfolio. Sources: Wikipedia, "Aphrodite" — …
sections.Vedic (graha): Shukra, son of the sage Bhṛgu, is guru to the asuras (as Bṛhaspati is guru to the devas) — Jyotiṣa's significator of love, marriage, beauty, and pleasure. His signature myth: austerities won him Sanjīvanī Vidyā from Śiva, the power to revive the dead, which he used to repeatedly resurrect fallen asuras in their war against the devas. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Shukra" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shukra; Mytho World, "Shukra — God of Venus and the Guru of Asuras" — …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Inanna (Akkadian Ishtar), among the oldest deities for whom written evidence survives, combined love, sex, and fertility with war and political power — an unusual pairing for a single figure. Her eight-pointed star marked her identification with Venus in both its "Morning Star" (warrior) and "Evening Star" (beauty) aspects; her myth of descending to the underworld and returning has been read as a mirror of Venus's own disappearance and reappearance in the sky. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Ishtar" — …
sections.What the lens reads: Love-goddess and war-goddess, teacher of demons with power to revive the dead, a beauty born from severed divinity in sea-foam — the throughline across three traditions is a bright, twin-aspected planet (morning star and evening star are literally the same body) mapped onto love, value, and attraction. The lens reads a real astronomical phenomenon — Venus's two appearances — through three unrelated symbol systems; none of the three is 'the' correct reading.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Mars

sections.Greco-Roman: Ares, son of Zeus and Hera, embodied war's raw violence and confusion — the Greeks themselves regarded him with distaste, one of their least-worshipped Olympians. Rome's Mars was a very different figure: second only to Jupiter in importance, more disciplined in portrayal, and doubling as an agricultural guardian — a war-and-harvest combination distinctive to early Roman religion. Rome formally identified Mars with Ares despite this temperamental gap. Sources: GreekReporter, "Ares vs. Mars" — …
sections.Vedic (graha): Mangala (also Aṅgāraka, "the red one") is Jyotiṣa's significator of courage, aggression, and drive — a fiery, challenging graha. Two competing origin myths exist: the Śaiva account has him born from three drops of Śiva's sweat, raised by the Earth-goddess Bhūmi; the Vaiṣṇava account ties his birth to Viṣṇu's boar-avatar Varāha piercing the Earth to rescue it, infusing it with divine essence. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Mangala" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala; Exotic India, "About …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Nergal, god of war, plague, and "inflicted death," began as a regional agricultural deity of the city of Kutha before becoming lord of the underworld — in the myth of Nergal and Ereshkigal, he descends to challenge her, and the two end up ruling the underworld jointly as husband and wife. He was closely associated with the noon sun and the deadly heat of the Mesopotamian dry season. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Nergal" — https://www.worldhistory.org/Nergal/; Britannica, "Nergal" — …
sections.What the lens reads: An unloved war-god the Greeks distrusted, an underworld king who won his throne by threatening its queen, a red graha born of sweat or a boar's tusk — every tradition reaches for violence, heat, and challenge to describe the same rust-red point of light. That convergence says something about shared human pattern-recognition (a reddish object read as blood, fire, conflict), not that Mars 'causes' anger.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Jupiter

sections.Greco-Roman: Zeus, son of Cronus and Rhea, ruled Olympus as sky-and-thunder god and "father of gods and men"; the Greek and Roman names for him (and the Vedic Dyaus, below) share an Indo-European root meaning "sky father." Rome's Jupiter inherited Zeus's role as king of the gods and god of sky, law, and order. Sources: Wikipedia, "Zeus" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeus; British Museum blog, "Gods and goddesses of the Greek and Roman pantheon" — https://www.britishmuseum.org/blog/gods-and-goddesses-greek-and-roman-pantheon …
sections.Vedic (graha): Bṛhaspati (also Guru), teacher of the devas as Shukra teaches the asuras, is Jyotiṣa's significator of wisdom, expansion, and ethics — "guru" literally meaning "heavy [with knowledge]." He appears already in the Ṛgveda (book 4, hymn 50), described as born from the first light and carrying a bow strung with Ṛta, cosmic order; later texts call him son of the sage Aṅgiras. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Brihaspati" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brihaspati (confidence: ○).
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Marduk began as a minor agricultural god of Babylon before Hammurabi's reign (c. 1792 BCE) elevated him to supreme sky-god and king of the pantheon. The Enūma Eliš epic tells how he defeated the primordial sea-goddess Tiamat and built the heavens and earth from her body — the mythic charter for Babylon's claim to cosmic and political centrality. Later astral texts equate him with the planet Jupiter. Sources: World History Encyclopedia, "Enuma Elish"; EBSCO Research Starters, "Marduk" — …
sections.What the lens reads: A thunder-king who overthrew his own father, a wisdom-teacher whose bowstring is cosmic order itself, a city-god who slew chaos and built the world from its corpse — three cultures independently cast their largest visible wandering star as the "biggest" kind of god: king, teacher, world-orderer. The size and brightness of Jupiter in the sky maps onto "bigness" of role across traditions that never spoke to each other.

passages.grammar_name: Planetary Myths — the same sky, many readings
passages.name: Saturn

sections.Greco-Roman: Kronos, youngest Titan, castrated his father Uranus and later swallowed his own children on hearing a prophecy he would be overthrown by one of them; Zeus, hidden by Rhea, survived to force his siblings back out and depose him. Beneath the horror-myth, Kronos was likely an older harvest-god — his festival, the Kronia, was a harvest celebration echoed by Rome's Saturnalia. Rome's Saturn kept this agricultural, golden-age, "time" association. Sources: Wikipedia, "Cronus" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronus; Theoi …
sections.Vedic (graha): Shani, son of Sūrya (the Sun) and his wife's shadow-double Chhāyā, is Jyotiṣa's grim significator of karma, justice, and time's slow reckoning — appointed, in later myth, to oversee everyone's karmic account without exception. His birth story says his first infant glance caused a solar eclipse, and that Sūrya himself could not bear to look at his dark-complexioned son directly. As taught in Jyotiṣa, summarized — Wikipedia, "Shani" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shani; Exotic India, "All About Shani Dev" — …
sections.Babylonian/Mesopotamian: Saturn's Mesopotamian layer is the least settled of the seven: 1st-millennium astral texts (e.g. MUL.APIN) equate Saturn with Ninurta, a farmer-and-war god, but earlier tradition (under the variant name Ninib) sometimes cast the same figure as a solar deity instead — a real ambiguity in the sources, not a settled one-to-one mapping. What's firmer: Ninurta's harvest-god role parallels Kronos's, plausibly why the Greek-to-Babylonian chain (Kronos = Saturn = Ninurta) held. Sources: Ancient Mesopotamia, "Ninurta" — …
sections.What the lens reads: A child-devouring Titan who was secretly a harvest-god, a karma-accountant whose own father couldn't bear to look at him, a Mesopotamian farmer-god whose "Saturn" identity even ancient scribes weren't fully consistent about — Saturn is the one planet where every tradition, including the oldest layer, treats the assignment as difficult and heavy. That the ancients themselves disagreed about which god belongs here is worth sitting with, not smoothing over.

sections.Interpretation: Saturn is the Greater Infortune, 'by universal experience acknowledged to be the most potent, evil, and malignant of all the planets.' Those born under him have 'small, black, leering eyes, thick lips and nostrils, large ears, thin face, lowering looks, cloudy aspect.' The most certain characteristic: 'he will never look thee in the face.' Chaucer summarizes: 'My loking is the fader of pestilence.'
sections.Light: Constant in friendship, laborious, patient, enduring—if you can endure him
sections.Shadow: Drowning, prison, strangling, rebellion, poisoning, ruin, cold diseases, dark treasons—'the fader of pestilence'

sections.Interpretation: Jupiter is 'the most propitious of all the planets, and the native born under his influence has every reason to be jovial in fact as he is by nature.' Such natives will be 'tall and fair, handsome and erect, robust, ruddy, and altogether a good-looking person.' Unless Jupiter is afflicted—then he denotes 'quacks and mountebanks, knaves, cheats, and drunkards.'
sections.Light: Judges, counsellors, church dignitaries, scholars, woollendrapers (possibly explaining the woolsack)
sections.Shadow: When afflicted: quacks, mountebanks, knaves, cheats, and drunkards—quite a fall from cardinals to drunkards

sections.Interpretation: Mars, the Lesser Infortune, makes natives 'of fierce countenance, his eyes sparkling, or sharp and darting, his complexion fiery or yellowish, and his countenance scarred or furrowed.' Hair color depends on sign: watery sign gives flaxen hair, earthy gives chestnut. 'The influence of Saturn may be compared to a lingering but fatal consumption; that of Mars to a burning fever.'
sections.Light: Generals, surgeons, barbers, smiths, sculptors, cooks—'all cut throat people'
sections.Shadow: When afflicted with Mercury or Moon: thieves, hangmen, and 'all cut throat people' (literally this time)

sections.Interpretation: The solar native has 'a round face (like pictures of the sun in old books of astronomy), with a short chin.' The Sun is 'the natural significator of respectability; for which I can discover no reason, unless it be that the sun travelling always in the ecliptic has no latitude, and so solar folk are allowed none.' When ill aspected: 'proud and mean, tyrannical and sycophantic.'
sections.Light: Emperors, kings, titled folk, goldsmiths, jewellers, coiners—the respectable (or those pretending to be)
sections.Shadow: When afflicted: 'pretenders either to power or knowledge'—arrogance and ignorant pomposity

sections.Interpretation: 'The native of Venus hath a love-dimple in the chin, a lovely mouth, cherry lips, and a right merry countenance.' Venus's benevolence was proven, according to Raphael (1828), by 'our present beloved monarch' George IV—'a most illustrious proof of the celestial science.' (George IV was notorious for dissipation, which Proctor notes with evident irony.)
sections.Light: Musicians, embroiderers, perfumers, classic modellers—those who administer to luxuries of the great
sections.Shadow: When afflicted: 'the lower orders of the votaries of voluptuousness'

sections.Interpretation: Mercury is 'a cold, dry, melancholy star.' The Mercurial has 'high forehead and thin sharp nose, thin beard (many times none at all), slender of body, and with small weak eyes.' When well affected: 'a strong, vigorous, active mind.' Long slender hands and fingers are 'especial marks of Mercury.'
sections.Light: Astrologers, philosophers, mathematicians, politicians, merchants, poets—all ingenious, clever men
sections.Shadow: When ill affected: pettifoggers, cunning vile persons, thieves, messengers, footmen, and servants

sections.Interpretation: The Moon's natives are 'of good stature, fair, and pale, moon-faced, with grey eyes, short arms, thick hands and feet, smooth, corpulent and phlegmatic body.' When in watery signs: 'he or she is blub-cheeked, not a handsome body, but a muddling creature.' 'Unless the moon is very well aspected, she ever signifies an ordinary vulgar person.'
sections.Light: Sailors, all persons connected with water or any kind of fluid, those in inferior and common offices
sections.Shadow: The muddling creature: blub-cheeked, ordinary, vulgar—unless very well aspected

sections.Interpretation: 'It is unfortunate for astrology that nothing was ever observed which seemed to suggest the possibility of an unknown planet. Astrologers tell us now that Uranus is a very potent planet; yet the old astrologers seem to have got on very well without him.' Raphael falsely claimed Halley and Bradley discovered Uranus through perturbation analysis—'Of course there is not a word of truth in this.'
sections.Light: If well aspected: profound in secret sciences, magnanimous, lofty of mind
sections.Shadow: Uranus is 'peculiarly hostile to' women, 'and very evil in love.' Beware marriage when Uranus afflicts!

sections.Interpretation: Aries is 'vernal, dry, fiery, masculine, cardinal, equinoctial, diurnal, movable, commanding, eastern, choleric, violent, and quadrupedalian.' It 'signifies a dry constitution, long face and neck, thick shoulders, swarthy complexion, and a hasty, passionate temper.' Governs head and face. Reigns over England, France, Germany, Syria, Naples, Verona.
sections.Light: Fortunate, commanding, initiating—the house of Mars at its most martial
sections.Shadow: Hasty, passionate, violent, choleric—'destruction by burning, and murder'

sections.Interpretation: Taurus 'gives to the native a stout athletic frame, broad bull-like forehead, dark curly hair, short neck, and so forth, and a dull apathetic temper, exceedingly cruel and malicious if once aroused.' Governs neck and throat. Reigns over Ireland, Holland, Persia, Leipzig. Feminine and unfortunate.
sections.Light: Stout, athletic, strong—physical power if nothing else
sections.Shadow: Dull, apathetic, but 'exceedingly cruel and malicious if once aroused'—the sleeping bull

sections.Interpretation: The native of Gemini will have 'sanguine complexion and tall, straight figure, dark eyes quick and piercing, brown hair, active ways, and will be of exceedingly ingenious intellect.' Governs arms and shoulders. Rules London (the great fire, plague, and London Bridge all occurred when Gemini was prominent—or so astrologers claim after the fact).
sections.Light: Ingenious intellect, quick eyes, active ways—Mercury's house at its best
sections.Shadow: Post-hoc reasoning: any major London event gets attributed to Gemini after it happens

sections.Interpretation: Cancer natives are 'of fair but pale complexion, round face, grey or mild blue eyes, weak voice, the upper part of the body large, slender arms, small feet, and an effeminate constitution.' Governs breast and stomach. Reigns over Scotland, Holland, Africa, Constantinople, New York. Feminine and unfortunate.
sections.Light: Fair complexion, grey eyes—the Moon's own sign
sections.Shadow: Effeminate constitution, weak voice—'indicative of all changeable and mutable circumstances'

sections.Interpretation: Leo natives are 'of large body, broad shoulders, austere countenance, with dark eyes and tawny hair, strong voice, and leonine character, resolute and ambitious, but generous, free, and courteous.' Governs heart and back. Reigns over Italy, France, Rome, Philadelphia. Masculine and fortunate.
sections.Light: Leonine character: resolute, ambitious, generous, free, courteous—the Sun's royal house
sections.Shadow: Austere countenance—royalty demands its distance

sections.Interpretation: Virgo natives 'are of moderate stature, seldom handsome, slender but compact, thrifty and ingenious.' Governs abdomen. Reigns over Turkey, Greece, Crete, Jerusalem, Paris, Lyons. Feminine and 'generally unfortunate.'
sections.Light: Thrifty, ingenious, compact—Mercury's practical house
sections.Shadow: Seldom handsome, generally unfortunate—the maid's modest lot

sections.Interpretation: Libra natives are 'tall and well made, elegant in person, round-faced and ruddy, but plain-featured and inclined to eruptions that disfigure the face when old; they are of sweet disposition, just and upright in dealing.' Governs lumbar regions. Reigns over Austria, Portugal, India, Vienna, Charleston. Masculine and fortunate.
sections.Light: Elegant, sweet disposition, just and upright—Venus brings beauty and balance
sections.Shadow: Plain-featured and 'inclined to eruptions that disfigure the face when old'—time comes for all

sections.Interpretation: Scorpio natives are 'strong, corpulent, and robust, with large bones, dark curly hair and eyes (presumably the eyes dark only, not curly), middle stature, dusky complexion, active bodies; they are usually reserved in speech.' Governs the groin. Feminine and unfortunate. '(It would appear likely, by the way, that astrology was a purely masculine science.)'
sections.Light: Strong, robust, active, reserved—Mars's nocturnal power
sections.Shadow: Proctor's aside: astrology consistently marks feminine signs as unfortunate—suspicious pattern

sections.Interpretation: Sagittarius natives are 'well formed and tall, ruddy, handsome, and jovial, with fine clear eyes, chestnut hair, and oval fleshy face. They are generally jolly fellows at either bin or board, active, intrepid, generous, and obliging.' Governs thighs. Masculine and 'of course fortunate.'
sections.Light: Jolly fellows at either bin or board—Jupiter's merry house
sections.Shadow: Of course fortunate—because masculine (Proctor notes the pattern)

sections.Interpretation: Capricorn gives 'a dry constitution and slender make, with a long thin visage, thin beard (a generally goaty aspect, in fact), dark hair, long neck, narrow chin, and weak knees. It governs, nevertheless, the knees and hams.' Reigns over India, Greece, Mexico, Oxford. Feminine and unfortunate.
sections.Light: Saturn's house of discipline and toil—there must be some virtue in that
sections.Shadow: A generally goaty aspect, weak knees—unfortunate being feminine, as usual

sections.Interpretation: Aquarius natives are 'robust, steady, strong, healthy, and of middle stature; delicate complexion, clear but not pale, sandy hair, hazel eyes, and generally an honest disposition.' Governs legs and ankles. Reigns over Russia, Denmark, Hamburg, Bremen. Masculine and fortunate.
sections.Light: Robust, honest, healthy—Saturn's better side in a masculine sign
sections.Shadow: Even Saturn produces fortunate results when the sign is masculine

sections.Interpretation: Pisces natives are 'short, pale, thick-set, and round-shouldered (like fish), its character phlegmatic and effeminate.' Governs feet and toes. Reigns over Portugal, Spain, Egypt, Normandy. 'It is feminine, and therefore, naturally, unfortunate.'
sections.Light: Jupiter's nocturnal house—some capacity for reverence and philosophy
sections.Shadow: Round-shouldered like fish, phlegmatic, effeminate—'feminine, and therefore, naturally, unfortunate'

sections.Interpretation: The Ascendant House, rising above the horizon at the east, 'was regarded as the House of Life, the planets located therein at the moment of birth having most potent influence on the life and destiny of the native.' From this comes our expression that something is 'in the ascendant.' Angular and powerful.
sections.Light: Life, destiny, beginnings—the most important house for the native
sections.Shadow: If malefics occupy, the native's life and health suffer from the start

sections.Interpretation: The House of Riches, 'one-third of the way from the east below the horizon towards the place of the sun at midnight.' Succedent, supporting the angular first house. Material sustenance follows life itself.
sections.Light: Riches, possessions, material security
sections.Shadow: Or poverty, if malefics are found here

sections.Interpretation: The House of Kindred, short journeys, letters, messages. Two-thirds of the way toward midnight. Cadent and weak in power, preparing for the fourth house angle.
sections.Light: Brothers, sisters, neighbors, communication, short travels
sections.Shadow: Cadent houses are weakest—kindred may offer little support

sections.Interpretation: The House of Parents, at the midnight position of the sun. Angular and powerful. 'The place of the sun at midnight'—foundations, ancestry, endings.
sections.Light: Parents, ancestry, lands, inheritance, the foundation of life
sections.Shadow: Also 'the end of matters'—where things conclude

sections.Interpretation: The House of Children and Women, 'also of all sorts of amusements, theatres, banquets, and merry-making.' Succedent, supporting the fourth house. The pleasures that spring from secure foundations.
sections.Light: Children, pleasure, creativity, amusement, theatres, banquets
sections.Shadow: Excessive merry-making can squander what foundations provide

sections.Interpretation: The House of Sickness. Cadent and weak. Service, labor, and the ailments that come with them. The house before the Descendant, preparing for partnership through service.
sections.Light: Service, daily work, health practices when well managed
sections.Shadow: Sickness, servitude—the trials before relationship

sections.Interpretation: The House of Love and Marriage, at the western horizon where the sun sets. Angular and powerful. 'Opposite to the first'—what completes us lies across from our self.
sections.Light: Marriage, partnership, love, contracts, committed relationships
sections.Shadow: Also 'death (if afflicted)'—marriage unto death, one way or another

sections.Interpretation: The House of Death, 'the first house above the horizon, lying to the west.' Succedent, following the seventh. What marriage shares: resources, intimacy, and ultimately mortality.
sections.Light: Inheritance, shared resources, transformation
sections.Shadow: Death, fear, anxiety, the goods of the dead

sections.Interpretation: The House of Religion, science, learning, books, and long voyages. 'Next to the mid-heaven on the west.' Cadent, preparing for the culminating tenth house. The wisdom sought before worldly achievement.
sections.Light: Religion, philosophy, higher learning, long journeys, divination
sections.Shadow: Cadent weakness—knowledge without power to apply it

sections.Interpretation: The Mid-heaven, 'the region occupied by the sun at midday.' Angular and most visible. 'The House of Honour, denoting credit, renown, profession or calling, trade, preferment.' The peak of worldly achievement.
sections.Light: Honor, profession, reputation, authority, achievement, visibility
sections.Shadow: Empty honor, reputation without substance, the loneliness of the peak

sections.Interpretation: The House of Friends, 'next to the mid-heaven on the east.' Succedent, supporting the tenth. The allies who gather around our public position.
sections.Light: Friends, hopes, benefactors, good fortune, future vision
sections.Shadow: False friends, hopes disappointed—those who attach to success

sections.Interpretation: The House of Enemies. Cadent and weak. 'Even Lilly himself was indicted in 1655 because he had given judgment respecting stolen goods—apparently the twelfth house, House of Enemies, had caught up with him.'
sections.Light: Solitude, retreat, hidden strengths, spiritual work
sections.Shadow: Hidden enemies, imprisonment, self-undoing—the house that catches up with astrologers

sections.Interpretation: When planets occupy the same degree, their powers unite—'whether for good or ill, according to the nature of the stars involved.' The most powerful configuration, for better or worse.
sections.Light: Fusion of powers, intensification, new beginnings
sections.Shadow: Malefics in conjunction magnify each other's harm

sections.Interpretation: Sixty degrees apart, 'comprehending two signs.' Considered friendly because signs in sextile 'share the same gender but differ in element, producing harmony through difference.'
sections.Light: Harmony through difference, friendly cooperation
sections.Shadow: Mild benefit only—not powerful enough to overcome serious affliction

sections.Interpretation: Ninety degrees apart, 'comprehending three signs.' Considered inharmonious because signs in square 'share the same modality but are of contrary elements.'
sections.Light: Tension that motivates action, crisis that builds strength
sections.Shadow: Conflict, obstacles, frustration—the difficult aspect

sections.Interpretation: One hundred twenty degrees apart, 'comprehending four signs.' Considered 'most harmonious and beneficial, as signs in trine share the same element and thus the same essential nature.'
sections.Light: Natural harmony, ease, blessing, grace
sections.Shadow: Gifts taken for granted, complacency, unrealized potential

sections.Interpretation: One hundred eighty degrees apart, 'comprehending six signs.' Produces 'disharmony through complete separation, as opposing signs are furthest apart and thus contrary in influence.'
sections.Light: Awareness through polarity, the tension that creates relationship
sections.Shadow: Separation, contrary influences, the pull of opposites

sections.Interpretation: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* Saturn produces cold and dryness, for he is most remote both from the Sun's heat and from the earth's vapours. But he is more effective in the production of cold than of dryness. Saturn is esteemed malefic, or causer of evil, from his excess of cold. The coldness of Saturn is allotted to the day, to counterbalance its heat.
sections.Light: When moderated by combination with day, Saturn produces a favourable temperament. His influence brings structure, time, and the wisdom of age and distance.
sections.Shadow: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — close restatement of the translated text, not an independent reading; the passage is quoted in "The record" below* Malefic, causer of evil from excess of cold. Saturn and Mars are esteemed of a contrary nature to the benefics, noxious in their influence.
sections.The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822): *Book I, Ch. IV–VII, on Saturn's temperament and sect (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):* > Saturn produces cold and dryness, for he is most remote both from the Sun's heat and from the earth's vapours. But he is more effective in the production of cold than of dryness. … Saturn and Mars are esteemed of a contrary nature, and malefic, or causers of evil: the first from his excess of cold, the other from his excess of dryness. … The Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are called masculine. … …

sections.Interpretation: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* Jupiter revolves in an intermediate sphere between the extreme cold of Saturn and the burning heat of Mars, and has consequently a temperate influence: he therefore at once promotes both warmth and moisture. But, owing to the spheres of Mars and the Sun, which lie beneath him, his warmth is predominant: and hence he produces fertilizing breezes.
sections.Light: Jupiter is considered by the ancients as benefic, or causer of good, because heat and moisture are predominant in him. He produces fertilizing breezes and promotes growth.
sections.Shadow: When afflicted, Jupiter's temperate nature may be overwhelmed by contrary influences, reducing his beneficial effects.
sections.The record — Ptolemy, tr. Ashmand (1822): *Book I, Ch. IV–VI, on Jupiter's temperament (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):* > Jupiter revolves in an intermediate sphere between the extreme cold of Saturn and the burning heat of Mars, and has consequently a temperate influence: he therefore at once promotes both warmth and moisture. But, owing to the spheres of Mars and the Sun, which lie beneath him, his warmth is predominant: and hence he produces fertilizing breezes. … [T]wo of the planets, on account of their temperate …

sections.Interpretation: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* Mars chiefly causes dryness, and is also strongly heating, by means of his own fiery nature, which is indicated by his colour, and in consequence of his vicinity to the Sun; the sphere of which is immediately below him. Mars is esteemed malefic from his excess of dryness.

sections.Shadow: Malefic, causer of evil from excess of dryness. His fiery nature, indicated by his colour, produces burning effects.

sections.Light: Venus is considered benefic, a causer of good, because her temperate quality promotes moisture. She is feminine, nocturnal, and brings harmony and fertility.
sections.Shadow: When afflicted, Venus's moistening influence may produce excess, leading to indulgence or dissolution.

sections.Light: Mercury is common to both genders, and common in influence—diurnal when matutine, nocturnal when vespertine. His rapid motion produces rapid changes.
sections.Shadow: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* Being excited by the velocity of his motion with the Sun, he consequently operates rapid changes tending to produce alternately either quality.

sections.Light: Aries initiates the cycle, provides the moisture of spring that introduces all other seasons. Cardinal fire energy that begins new cycles.
sections.Shadow: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* The stars in the head of Aries possess an influence similar in its effects to that of Mars and Saturn—both malefics.

sections.Interpretation: Taurus is a fixed sign that follows the equinoctial Aries. During the Sun's presence in fixed signs, the cold, heat, moisture or dryness of the season is more firmly established. Those stars in Taurus in the abscission of the sign resemble the influence of Venus.
sections.Light: Fixed earth that stabilizes what the equinoctial sign initiated. The Pleiades within bring lunar and martial influence.
sections.Shadow: *Ptolemy, tr. J. M. Ashmand (1822) — close restatement of the translated text, not an independent reading; the passage is quoted in "The record" below* The Hyades star which is bright and ruddy, called Facula, has the same temperament as Mars—a malefic influence within the sign.

Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* Gemini is a bicorporeal sign, intermediately placed between the fixed and tropical signs, participating in the constitutional properties of both. The stars in the feet of Gemini have an influence similar to that of Mercury, and moderately to that of Venus.
sections.Light: Mutable air that transitions between seasons, carrying properties of both fixed and cardinal. Mercury's house of communication and duality.
sections.Shadow: The two bright stars on the heads—Apollo like Mercury, Hercules like Mars—show the dual nature can tend toward conflict.

Ashmand (1822) — close restatement of the translated text, not an independent reading; the passage is quoted in "The record" below* The Moon's domicile, where lunar influence is strongest. sections.Light: Fixed fire that establishes the heat of summer. Regulus brings the combined fortune of Mars's courage and Jupiter's expansion.

sections.Light: Mutable earth transitioning from summer to autumn. Mercury's exaltation and joy, bringing intellectual refinement to practical matters.

sections.Light: Fixed water that consolidates the descent into darkness. Mars's nocturnal domicile bringing transformative intensity.
sections.Shadow: The bright stars near the front, and those in the body, are similar to Mars and partly to Saturn—double malefic influence.

sections.Interpretation: Sagittarius is a bicorporeal sign, participating in the properties of both fixed and tropical signs. Jupiter's domicile, bringing the expansive influence of the greater benefic to the mutable fire.
sections.Light: Mutable fire transitioning from autumn to winter, carrying both established and initiating properties. Jupiter's philosophical expansion.

sections.Light: Cardinal earth initiating the return of light after the winter solstice. Saturn's discipline and structure in its domicile.
sections.Shadow: Saturn's nocturnal house where his cold, dry, malefic nature is most established. Mars is exalted here, adding martial intensity.

sections.Interpretation: Aquarius is a fixed sign following the winter solstice. Saturn's diurnal domicile, where his cold influence is moderated by the day. Fixed air that establishes the patterns of winter.
sections.Light: Fixed air consolidating winter's lessons. Saturn's diurnal house where coldness is tempered by daylight hours.
sections.Shadow: Saturn's house still carries malefic potential, though moderated by its diurnal nature.

sections.Interpretation: Pisces is a bicorporeal sign, the last of the zodiac, participating in the properties of both fixed and tropical signs. Jupiter's nocturnal domicile and Venus's exaltation bring benefic influence to the mutable water.
sections.Light: Mutable water dissolving winter and preparing for spring's renewal. Jupiter and Venus both have dignity here, doubling benefic influence.
sections.Shadow: The bright star at the binding of the two fishes is like Mars, and moderately like Mercury—martial dissolution present.

sections.Interpretation: The Ascendant, also called the Horoscope (Greek: Horoskopos), is the portion rising above the horizon at the east. Planets here have the most potent influence on the life and destiny of the native. The Ascendant is considered masculine and the first of the masculine signs.
sections.Light: Life, body, soul, constitution—the very self of the native. Angular and most powerful position.
sections.Shadow: Malefics here afflict the native's life and health from birth.

sections.Interpretation: The Subterranean angle (Greek: Hypogeion) is the lower heaven, the place of the midnight Sun. It signifies parents, ancestry, foundations, and the end of matters.
sections.Light: Roots, home, ancestry, the foundation upon which life is built. Angular and powerful.
sections.Shadow: Also signifies the end of matters—where things conclude.

sections.Interpretation: The Descendant or Occidental angle (Greek: Dysis) is opposite the Ascendant, the place where stars set. It signifies marriage, partnerships, and open dealings with others.
sections.Light: Partnership, marriage, contracts—the complementary other that completes the self.
sections.Shadow: Also signifies open enemies and, when afflicted, death.

sections.Interpretation: The Mid-heaven or Culmination (Greek: Mesouranema) is the southern angle, the highest point of the heavens, where the Sun reaches at noon. It signifies honour, profession, authority, and public reputation.
sections.Light: Career, reputation, public standing, the heights one may achieve. Angular and most visible position.
sections.Shadow: Empty honors, reputation without substance, the isolation of the peak.

sections.Interpretation: The conjunction occurs when planets occupy the same degree. Ptolemy does not include conjunction among the aspects proper, since a part of the zodiac cannot be configurated with itself, but its efficacy is frequently adverted to throughout the work.
sections.Light: Fusion, unity, intensification—the most powerful configuration for blending planetary influences.
sections.Shadow: Malefics in conjunction magnify each other's harm. The distinction between planets is lost.

sections.Light: Harmony through compatible difference. Signs in sextile share the same gender but differ in element.
sections.Shadow: Mild benefit only—not powerful enough to overcome serious affliction.

sections.Light: Dynamic tension that motivates action. Crisis that builds character through challenge.
sections.Shadow: Discordant configuration between signs of different natures and sexes. Conflict and obstacles.

sections.Light: Most harmonious and beneficial aspect. Signs in trine share the same element and thus the same essential nature.
sections.Shadow: Gifts taken for granted. Ease may lead to complacency and unrealized potential.

Ashmand (1822) — excerpted verbatim; the fuller passage is quoted in "The record" below* The opposition attaches to all parts diametrically distant from each other, containing between them two right angles, or six signs, or a hundred and eighty degrees. The opposition is considered to be discordant because it is a configuration made between signs of different natures.
sections.Light: Awareness through polarity. The tension that creates relationship and completion.
sections.Shadow: Discordant configuration between contrary signs. Separation, conflict, the pull of opposites.

XVI, and Ashmand's footnote (excerpted, fetched from sacred-texts.com; … marks elisions):* > This mutual configuration attaches to all parts diametrically distant from each other, containing between them two right angles, or six signs, or a hundred and eighty degrees … the distance by diameter is in itself sufficiently clear, and requires no further explanation. … The opposition and quartile are considered to be discordant, because they are configurations made between signs not of the same kind, but …

sections.Story: The Sun is your core identity — who you are becoming. It represents your conscious will, creative force, and the central organizing principle of your life.
sections.Light: Vitality, self-expression, leadership, creative power, confidence, generosity.
sections.Shadow: Ego inflation, domination, burnout from over-identification with achievement.
sections.Archetype: The King/Queen — sovereign consciousness that gives light and warmth.

sections.Story: The Moon is your emotional body — how you feel, what you need, and where you seek comfort. It governs your instinctual responses and your relationship to home, nurturing, and memory.
sections.Light: Emotional intelligence, receptivity, nurturing, intuition, responsiveness.
sections.Shadow: Moodiness, dependency, emotional overwhelm, clinging to the past.
sections.Archetype: The Mother — the container that holds and nourishes life.

sections.Story: Mercury is the mind in motion — how you think, communicate, and make sense of the world. It governs language, learning, commerce, and the bridges between things.
sections.Light: Articulate, curious, adaptable, quick-witted, perceptive.
sections.Shadow: Overthinking, trickery, scattered attention, nervousness.
sections.Archetype: The Messenger — the one who carries meaning between worlds.

sections.Story: Venus is what you love, what you value, and how you attract. She governs beauty, pleasure, relationship, aesthetics, and the principle of harmony.
sections.Light: Grace, magnetism, aesthetic sense, diplomacy, devotion.
sections.Shadow: Vanity, possessiveness, people-pleasing, overindulgence.
sections.Archetype: The Lover — the force that draws things together through beauty.

sections.Story: Mars is your drive, desire, and fighting spirit. It governs how you assert yourself, pursue what you want, and handle conflict and competition.
sections.Light: Courage, initiative, passion, decisiveness, physical vitality.
sections.Shadow: Aggression, impatience, recklessness, anger, domination.
sections.Archetype: The Warrior — the force that cuts through and takes action.

sections.Story: Jupiter is expansion, meaning, and faith. It governs your search for truth, your sense of abundance, and your capacity for growth, wisdom, and joy.
sections.Light: Generosity, optimism, wisdom, philosophical depth, good fortune.
sections.Shadow: Excess, overconfidence, dogmatism, restlessness, waste.
sections.Archetype: The Sage — the one who sees the larger pattern and offers meaning.

sections.Story: Saturn is structure, time, and responsibility. It governs your relationship to limits, mastery, maturity, and the hard-won wisdom that comes from endurance.
sections.Light: Discipline, integrity, perseverance, mastery, wisdom through experience.
sections.Shadow: Rigidity, fear, depression, excessive control, self-denial.
sections.Archetype: The Elder — the keeper of boundaries who teaches through limitation.

sections.Story: Uranus is the awakener — sudden insight, revolution, and liberation from the old. It governs innovation, eccentricity, and the impulse to break free.
sections.Light: Originality, genius, liberation, humanitarian vision, breakthrough.
sections.Shadow: Rebellion without cause, detachment, instability, contrarianism.
sections.Archetype: The Revolutionary — the lightning bolt that shatters old forms.

sections.Story: Neptune dissolves boundaries — between self and other, real and imagined, sacred and mundane. It governs dreams, spirituality, compassion, and the longing to merge with something greater.
sections.Light: Compassion, imagination, spiritual devotion, artistic vision, transcendence.
sections.Shadow: Delusion, addiction, escapism, victimhood, confusion.
sections.Archetype: The Mystic — the one who sees through the veil.

sections.Story: Pluto is the force of transformation — death, rebirth, and the confrontation with power in its rawest form. It governs the underworld of the psyche and the process of radical change.
sections.Light: Transformation, regeneration, depth psychology, empowerment, truth.
sections.Shadow: Obsession, manipulation, power struggles, destructiveness.
sections.Archetype: The Alchemist — the one who transforms through descent into the depths.

sections.Story: The North Node points to your evolutionary direction — the unfamiliar territory your soul is growing toward in this lifetime. It feels uncomfortable precisely because it is new.
sections.Light: Growth edge, soul purpose, future direction, evolutionary calling.
sections.Shadow: Overreaching, anxiety about the unknown, spiritual bypassing.
sections.Archetype: The Compass — pointing toward what you came here to learn.

sections.Story: The South Node represents what you already know — gifts, patterns, and tendencies carried from the past. Mastery here is the foundation, but over-reliance becomes a trap.
sections.Light: Natural talent, deep familiarity, comfort zone, karmic gifts.
sections.Shadow: Stagnation, regression, repeating old patterns, avoiding growth.
sections.Archetype: The Ancestor — the inherited wisdom that can become a prison.

sections.Story: Chiron is the wound that becomes a gift. It shows where you carry a deep, often early wound — and where your greatest capacity to heal others lives.
sections.Light: Healing wisdom, mentorship, bridging worlds, compassionate teaching.
sections.Shadow: Chronic pain, feeling broken, avoiding the wound, over-identification with suffering.
sections.Archetype: The Wounded Healer — the one whose wound becomes medicine.

sections.Story: Aries is the spark of initiation — the first fire, the impulse to exist. Here energy moves before thought, asserting itself into being.
sections.Light: Courage, initiative, authenticity, pioneering spirit, directness.
sections.Shadow: Impatience, selfishness, combativeness, recklessness.
sections.Archetype: The Pioneer — first to arrive, first to act.

sections.Story: Taurus is embodiment — the pleasure of having form, of touching earth, of building something that lasts. Here spirit takes root in matter.
sections.Light: Stability, sensuality, patience, resourcefulness, loyalty.
sections.Shadow: Stubbornness, possessiveness, materialism, resistance to change.
sections.Archetype: The Builder — the one who gives form to what matters.

sections.Story: Gemini is the dance of duality — the mind that plays with ideas, makes connections, and refuses to be pinned to a single truth. Here reality becomes conversation.
sections.Light: Versatility, wit, curiosity, communication, adaptability.
sections.Shadow: Superficiality, inconsistency, gossip, restlessness.
sections.Archetype: The Storyteller — the one who gives voice to multiplicity.

sections.Story: Cancer is the shell and the softness within — the impulse to protect, nourish, and create a container for vulnerability. Here the emotional body becomes home.
sections.Light: Nurturing, emotional depth, protectiveness, tenacity, memory.
sections.Shadow: Clinginess, moodiness, defensiveness, emotional manipulation.
sections.Archetype: The Nurturer — the one who creates sanctuary.

sections.Story: Leo is the radiance of the creative self — the heart that shines, performs, and celebrates being alive. Here consciousness becomes an art form.
sections.Light: Creativity, generosity, warmth, leadership, self-expression.
sections.Shadow: Pride, attention-seeking, drama, stubbornness.
sections.Archetype: The Performer — the one whose light calls others to their own.

sections.Story: Virgo is devotion to craft — the sacred attention to detail, the impulse to refine, heal, and serve. Here consciousness meets the world through care.
sections.Light: Discernment, service, practical wisdom, humility, healing.
sections.Shadow: Perfectionism, criticism, anxiety, self-doubt.
sections.Archetype: The Healer — the one who makes whole through attention.

sections.Story: Libra is the art of relationship — the search for balance, beauty, and justice in the space between self and other. Here consciousness becomes dialogue.
sections.Light: Harmony, fairness, aesthetic sense, diplomacy, partnership.
sections.Shadow: Indecision, people-pleasing, avoidance of conflict, dependency.
sections.Archetype: The Artist — the one who creates beauty in the between.

sections.Story: Scorpio is the descent — the willingness to go where others won't, to face death, desire, and the raw truth of power. Here consciousness transforms through intensity.
sections.Light: Depth, passion, loyalty, psychological insight, regeneration.
sections.Shadow: Jealousy, manipulation, obsession, vindictiveness.
sections.Archetype: The Shaman — the one who travels between worlds.

sections.Story: Sagittarius is the arrow in flight — the search for meaning, truth, and horizons beyond the known. Here consciousness expands through vision and adventure.
sections.Light: Optimism, philosophy, adventure, generosity, truthfulness.
sections.Shadow: Dogmatism, excess, restlessness, bluntness, irresponsibility.
sections.Archetype: The Explorer — the one who follows the arrow of meaning.

sections.Story: Capricorn is the mountain — the slow, determined climb toward mastery and legacy. Here consciousness meets time, structure, and the weight of responsibility.
sections.Light: Ambition, discipline, integrity, practical wisdom, authority.
sections.Shadow: Coldness, workaholism, pessimism, rigidity, status obsession.
sections.Archetype: The Elder — the one who builds what endures.

sections.Story: Aquarius is the vision of what could be — the impulse toward collective evolution, individual freedom, and the future. Here consciousness serves the whole through radical originality.
sections.Light: Vision, humanitarianism, originality, intellectual independence.
sections.Shadow: Detachment, contrarianism, emotional avoidance, superiority.
sections.Archetype: The Visionary — the one who sees the future in the present.

sections.Story: Pisces is the ocean — the dissolution of separate self into the infinite. Here consciousness merges with everything, swimming in compassion, imagination, and the dream of unity.
sections.Light: Compassion, imagination, spirituality, artistic sensitivity, transcendence.
sections.Shadow: Escapism, victimhood, confusion, boundary dissolution.
sections.Archetype: The Dreamer — the one who remembers what the world has forgotten.

sections.Story: The house of self and emergence. How you appear, how you begin, how you enter a room and a life. The mask that becomes the face.
sections.Light: Self-awareness, physical vitality, personal initiative.
sections.Shadow: Self-absorption, identity crises, over-concern with image.

sections.Story: The house of resources and values. What you possess, what possesses you, and what you consider worth having. Your relationship to material reality.
sections.Light: Self-worth, material security, talent, sensory pleasure.
sections.Shadow: Greed, insecurity, over-attachment to possessions.

sections.Story: The house of communication and mind. How you speak, write, learn, and connect with your immediate environment. The neighborhood of consciousness.
sections.Light: Curiosity, articulation, mental agility, sibling bonds.
sections.Shadow: Gossip, scattered thinking, superficial connections.

sections.Story: The house of roots and foundation. Your home, your family of origin, your emotional bedrock. The place you return to when everything else falls away.
sections.Light: Emotional security, ancestry, belonging, inner foundation.
sections.Shadow: Family wounds, rootlessness, clinging to the past.

sections.Story: The house of creation and play. Where you make things for the joy of making them — children, art, romance, games. The stage where your heart performs.
sections.Light: Creative expression, romance, children, joy, risk-taking.
sections.Shadow: Drama addiction, gambling, narcissistic expression.

sections.Story: The house of service and daily practice. How you maintain your body, refine your craft, and serve the world through ordinary devotion. The sacred mundane.
sections.Light: Service, health awareness, craftsmanship, daily ritual.
sections.Shadow: Workaholism, hypochondria, perfectionism, servitude.

sections.Story: The house of the other. Your partnerships, marriages, open enemies, and projections. The mirror in which you see what you cannot see alone.
sections.Light: Partnership, commitment, diplomacy, balance through relationship.
sections.Shadow: Codependency, projection, loss of self in others.

sections.Story: The house of transformation and shared resources. Where you merge with others — financially, sexually, psychologically. The territory of death, inheritance, and rebirth.
sections.Light: Psychological depth, intimacy, shared power, transformation.
sections.Shadow: Power struggles, obsession, fear of loss, manipulation.

sections.Story: The house of expansion and meaning. Your philosophy, long journeys, higher education, and relationship to truth. Where you search for the big picture.
sections.Light: Wisdom, faith, cross-cultural understanding, philosophical depth.
sections.Shadow: Dogmatism, restlessness, spiritual bypassing, arrogance.

sections.Story: The house of vocation and public life. Your career, reputation, and contribution to the world. The peak of the chart — what you are seen to do.
sections.Light: Purpose, achievement, public contribution, authority.
sections.Shadow: Status obsession, workaholism, empty ambition, fear of failure.

sections.Story: The house of community and vision. Your friends, networks, hopes, and the groups you belong to. Where individual purpose meets collective dreaming.
sections.Light: Community, friendship, humanitarian ideals, innovation.
sections.Shadow: Conformity, detachment, misplaced idealism, loneliness in crowds.

sections.Story: The house of the unseen. Your unconscious, your connection to the collective dream, your hidden strengths and sorrows. The place before birth and after death.
sections.Light: Spiritual depth, compassion, artistic vision, surrender, healing.
sections.Shadow: Self-undoing, isolation, addiction, martyrdom, hidden enemies.

sections.Story: Two planets merge — their energies fuse into a single intensified force. Neither can be seen without the other. This is union, for better and worse.
sections.Light: Concentrated power, unified purpose, amplified expression.
sections.Shadow: Blind spots from over-identification, inability to separate energies.

sections.Story: Two planets face each other across the chart — a full-moon tension between polarities. The challenge is integration, not choosing sides.
sections.Light: Awareness through contrast, balance, objectivity, partnership dynamics.
sections.Shadow: Projection, polarization, seesaw between extremes.

sections.Story: Two planets flow together effortlessly — gifts that come naturally, talents that feel easy. The risk is taking them for granted.
sections.Light: Natural talent, ease, creative flow, harmony.
sections.Shadow: Complacency, laziness, wasted potential, taking gifts for granted.

sections.Story: Two planets clash at a right angle — creating friction, challenge, and ultimately growth. Squares are where the work is.
sections.Light: Motivation, dynamic tension, breakthrough, strength through challenge.
sections.Shadow: Chronic frustration, internal conflict, crisis patterns.

sections.Story: Two planets extend a hand — an opportunity aspect that requires a small effort to activate. The door is open but you must walk through it.
sections.Light: Opportunity, communication between energies, creative potential.
sections.Shadow: Missed opportunities from passivity, unrealized potential.

sections.Story: Two planets that have nothing in common — no element, no modality, no angle of recognition. The adjustment is perpetual, the integration creative and strange.
sections.Light: Creative adaptation, integrating the incompatible, resourcefulness.
sections.Shadow: Chronic adjustment fatigue, health issues from unresolved tension.

sections.What Lilly reads: Saturn as slow, pale, and socially low — the planet of age, poverty, and solitary labour rather than the 'great teacher' softening later 20th-century astrology gives him (see grammars/western-astrology-canonical). Lilly's Saturn is unambiguously the era's grimmest planet, not yet rehabilitated.
sections.Lilly's own words: "Saturn is the supreamest or highest of all the Planets... he is not very bright or glorious, but is of a Pale, Wan, or Leaden, Ashy colour, and slow in motion." On who he signifies: "In general Saturn signifies Husbandmen, Clowns, Beggars, Day-labourers, Old men, Fathers, Grand-fathers, Monks, Jesuits, Sectarists..." among many other lowly and solitary trades. (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, retaining Lilly's own spelling; confidence: ○ — corroborated across multiple secondary reproductions of the …
