sections.What Lilly reads: This is the era's most unreserved character portrait — Jupiter as moral excellence itself, virtue catalogued almost as a checklist. Compare Ptolemy's cooler, physics-of-temperature Jupiter (grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand) and Alan Leo's spiritualized Jupiter (grammars/alan-leo): three centuries apart, three quite different registers for 'the benefic.'
sections.Lilly's own words: Of the well-placed Jupiterian person: "Magnanimous, Faithfull, Bashfull, Aspiring in an honourable way at high matters, in all his actions a Lover of fair Dealing, desiring to benefit all men, doing Glorious things, Honourable and Religious, of sweet and affable Conversation, wonderfully indulgent to his Wife and Children, reverencing Aged men, a great Reliever of the Poor, full of Charity and Godlinesse, Liberal, hating all Sordid actions, Just, Wise, Prudent, Thankfull, Vertuous." (Quoted from Christian …
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Lilly opens the Jupiter chapter with the planet's classical names, then reaches, later in the same chapter, for the mirror-image of the virtuous Jupiterian already quoted above — his own historical judgment of the planet gone wrong, offered here as his voice, not a reading of the reader: “He is placed next to Saturn (amongst the Ancients) you shall sometimes find him called Zeus, or Phaeton: he is the greatest in appearance to our eyes of all the Planets (the Sun and Moon excepted); in his Colour he is bright …

sections.What Lilly reads: Mars-as-choler is the era's own humoral medicine speaking through the planet: hot, dry, red, quick to anger, prone to iron-wounds and inflammation. This is a physiological Mars as much as a psychological one, in a way pre-modern medicine and astrology genuinely shared one vocabulary for.
sections.Lilly's own words: "Mars is a masculine, nocturnal planet, in nature hot and dry, choleric and fiery; the lesser infortune, author of quarrels, strifes, and contentions." Physically: "martialists generally are of middle stature, their bodies strong, their bones large, rather lean than fat; their complexion of a brown, ruddy colour, their visage round, their hair red or sandy... sharp, hazel, piercing eyes; a bold confident countenance." On sickness: "Mars causes all hurts by iron, the shingles, and such other diseases as arise by …
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Past the temperament and physiology already quoted above, Lilly's chapter turns to Mars in two further registers — the martial virtue and the martial vice, both his own era's reading of the same hot, dry nature: “In feats of War and Courage invincible, scorning any should exceed him, subject to no Reason, Bold, Confident, Immovable, Contentious, challenging all Honour to themselves. Valiant, lovers of War and things pertaining thereunto, hazarding himself to all Perils, willingly will obey no body, or submit to …

sections.What Lilly reads: The Sun's significations here are an unbroken ladder of rank — king down through every grade of gentleman and courtier — with no separate psychological or emotional register at all. In this text the Sun IS social position; nothing about 'identity' or 'ego' in the modern sense the tropical-canonical library uses (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical).
sections.Lilly's own words: "He signifies kings, princes, emperors, &c.; dukes, marquisses, earls, barons, lieutenants, deputy lieutenants of counties, magistrates, gentlemen in general, courtiers, desirers of honour and preferment." (From Zadkiel's 1852 abridgment, An Introduction to Astrology, Chapter VIII, 'Of the Sun, His General and Particular Significations' — a public-domain modernized-spelling reprint tradition of Lilly's material, not a claim that these are Lilly's exact 1647 words; confidence: ○.)
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): The chapter already quoted above for the Sun's ranks-and-titles significations continues into character — Lilly's own two faces of the 'Solar man,' offered as a historical reading, not a claim on anyone born under the Sun: “Then the Solar man is Arrogant and Proud, disdaining all men, cracking of his Pedigree, he is Pur-blind in Sight and Judgment, restless, troublesome, domineering, a mere vapour, expensive, foolish, endued with no gravity in words, or soberness in Actions, a Spend-thrift, wasting his Patrimony …

sections.What Lilly reads: Venus's trade-list — musicians, silk-men, painters, jewellers, wives, choristers — reads almost as an occupational census of beauty-and-pleasure work in 17th-century London, a very concrete, tradesman's-eye-view Venus quite unlike the abstract 'love and harmony' of later psychological astrology (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical).
sections.Lilly's own words: A well-placed Venerian person is "a pretty, compleat, handsome Man or Woman" (if Oriental) or, if Occidental, of shorter stature yet "very decent and comely in Shape and Form, wel liked of all" — with "a stedfast eye, and full of amorous enticements." Venus governs "Musitions, Gamesters, Silk-men, Mercers, Linnen-Drapers, Painters, Jewellers, Players, Lapidaries, Embroiderers, Women-tailors, Wives, Mothers, Virgins, Choristers, Fidlers, Pipers." Her diseases are "principally in the Matrix and members of …
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Lilly's Venus chapter, not yet drawn on elsewhere in this item, gives its own two-sided moral portrait — pleasant sociability against its ill-dignified excess, presented here as the era's reading, not a script: “She is a Feminine Planet, temperately Cold and Moist, Nocturnal, the lesser Fortune, author of Mirth and Jollity… She signifies a quiet man, not given to Law, Quarrel or Wrangling; not Vicious, Pleasant, Neat and Spruce, loving Mirth in his words and actions, cleanly in Apparel… prone to Venery, often …

sections.What Lilly reads: 'Author of subtilty, tricks, devices, perjury' is a considerably darker Mercury than the Hellenistic 'common, convertible' planet (grammars/tetrabiblos-ashmand) or the Vedic Budha's speech-and-cleverness portfolio (grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka) — Lilly's 17th-century English Mercury leans hard toward the trickster and the liar, a moralizing gloss the other two traditions' texts don't emphasize as strongly.
sections.Lilly's own words: Mercury "rules the animal spirit: he is author of subtilty, tricks, devices, perjury, &c." — his nature convertible, taking on the quality of whatever planet he associates with, fittingly for a planet Lilly elsewhere treats as neither wholly masculine nor feminine, neither fully fortunate nor unfortunate. (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I; confidence: ○.)
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Lilly's Mercury opens with the planet's classical names and its odd genderlessness, then gives its own well- and ill-dignified pair, in his own moralizing register: “It is called Hermes, Stilbon, Cyllenius, Archas. Mercury is the least of all the Planets… We may not call him either Masculine or Feminine, for he is either the one or other as joined to any Planet: if in conjunction with a Masculine Planet, he becomes Masculine; if with a Feminine then Feminine; but of his own nature he is cold and dry, and therefore …

sections.What Lilly reads: This is a startlingly unflattering physical portrait next to the gentler, nurturing Moon of later astrology (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical) — swelling, watery-eyed, boar-toothed. Lilly's Moon-native description reads more like a period medical case-note on phlegmatic humoral excess than a psychological temperament sketch; the vividness is the point of reading him at all.
sections.Lilly's own words: A Moon-dominant person appears "in a great and full body, soft and phlegmatic, of colour like a black obscure cloud, having a swelling countenance, with eyes red and full of water, a bald head, and teeth like a wilde boar." (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I; confidence: ○ — corroborated across secondary reproductions this session.)
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): The Moon chapter opens with her ancient names before turning to manners — Lilly's own reading of the Moon's changeable temper, well- and ill-placed: “The Moon we find called by the Ancients, Lucina, Cynthia, Diana, Phoebe, Latona, Noctiluca, Proserpina; she is the nearest to the Earth of all the Planets… She is a Feminine, Nocturnal Planet, Cold, Moist and Phlegmatic.” Well placed: “She signifieth one of composed Manners, a soft, tender creature, a Lover of all honest and ingenious Sciences, a Searcher of and …

sections.In the text: “Aries is a Masculine, Diurnall Sign, moveable, Cardinall, Equinoctiall; in nature fiery, hot and dry, cholerick, bestial, luxurious, intemperate and violent: the diurnall house of Mars of the Fiery Triplicity, and of the East.” (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, the chapter on Aries; confidence: medium — identical wording corroborated across two independent secondary reproductions this session, chronosspeaks.com's Lilly sign digest and renaissanceastrology.com's Aries page.)
sections.What this lens reads: Lilly's Aries is a humoral-physical formula — masculine, hot, dry, choleric, prone to violence and excess — not yet the modern 'Pioneer' light/shadow archetype (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical); virtue and vice both sit inside the same hot, dry temperament rather than a separate moral register.
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): The same chapter that gives Aries's opening formula (quoted above) continues into the concrete grid horary astrology reads a chart through — disease, place, and body, offered here as Lilly's period taxonomy, not a diagnosis: “All Pushes, Wheals, Pimples in the Face, small Pocks, sore Lips, Polypus… Ringworms, Falling-sickness, Apoplexies, Megrims, Tooth-ache, Head-ache and Baldness.” Of places: “Where Sheep and small Cattle do feed or use to be, sandy and hilly Grounds, a place of refuge for Thieves… a Stable for …

sections.In the text: “Taurus is an Earthly, Cold, Dry, Melancholy, Feminine, Nocturnal, Fixed, Domestical or Beastial Sign, of the Earthly Triplicity, and South, the Night-house of Venus.” (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, the chapter on Taurus; confidence: medium — corroborated across chronosspeaks.com's Lilly sign digest and a second independent secondary reproduction this session.)
sections.What this lens reads: Lilly's Taurus is 'melancholy' and 'domestical/beastial' — a fixed-earth, cold-and-dry temperament rooted in the home and the beast-yard, not the sensuous 'Builder' of pleasure and stability that the modern light/shadow grammar gives it (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical); this supersedes the app's earlier generic AI-drafted 'Taurus' item, which had no primary-source grounding.
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Past the elemental formula already quoted for Taurus, the same chapter gives its diseases, places and bodily description: “The King's Evil, sore Throats, Wens, Fluxes of Rheums falling into the Throat, Quinsies, Imposthumes in those parts.” Of places: “Stables where Horses are, low Houses, Houses where the implements of Cattle are laid up, Pasture or Feeding grounds where no Houses are near.” Of the body: “It presents one of a short, but of a full, strong and well-set stature, a broad Forehead, great Eyes, big …

sections.In the text: “Gemini is an aerial, hot, moyst, sanguine, Diurnal, common or double-bodied human Sign; the diurnall house of Mercury of the aery triplicity, Western, Masculine.” (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, the chapter on Gemini, with two OCR-mangled words in the secondary mirrors — 'dounle' and 'Mascu1ine' — silently corrected to 'double' and 'Masculine' for legibility; confidence: medium — the same wording surfaced across two independent reproductions this session.)
sections.What this lens reads: Lilly's Gemini is a 'common or double-bodied human Sign' under Mercury — the mutable, airy, sanguine formula that later psychological astrology keeps almost unchanged as 'the Messenger' (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical), one of the closer continuities across this library rather than a sharp break.
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Continuing past Gemini's opening formula already quoted above, into diseases, places and body: “He signifies all Diseases or infirmities in the Arms, Shoulders, Hands, corrupted Blood, Windiness in the Veins, distempered Fancies.” Of places: “Wainscot Rooms, Plastering and Walls of Houses, the Halls, or where Play is used, Hills and Mountains, Barns, Storehouses for Corn, Coffers, Chests, High Places.” Of the body: “An upright, tall, straight Body either in Man or Woman, the Complexion sanguine, not clear, but …

sections.In the text: “Cancer is the onely house of the Moon, and is the first Sign of the Watry or Northern Triplicity, is Watry, Cold, Moyst, Flegmatick, Feminine, Nocturnal, Moveable, a Solstice Sign mute and slow of Voyce, Fruitful, Northern.” (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, the chapter on Cancer; confidence: medium — identical wording corroborated across two independent secondary reproductions this session.)
sections.What this lens reads: 'Mute and slow of Voyce' and 'Flegmatick' is Lilly's Cancer speaking the era's humoral medicine as much as its astrology, a fruitful but wordless watery sign quite unlike the nurturing, emotionally expressive Cancer of later astrology (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical) and Jyotiṣa's own watery, Moon-ruled Karkaṭa (grammars/jyotisa-brhat-jataka).
sections.The record — William Lilly (1647): Past the formula already quoted for Cancer, the chapter turns to disease, place and body: “It signifies Imperfections all over, or in the Breast, Stomach and Paps, weak Digestion, cold Stomach, Ptisick, salt Phlegms, rotten Coughs, dropsical Humours, Imposthumations in the Stomach, Cancers which ever are in the Breast.” Of places: “The Sea, great Rivers, Navigable Waters; but in the Inland Countries it notes places near Rivers, Brooks, Springs, Wells, Cellars in Houses, Wash-houses, Marsh grounds, Ditches with …

sections.In the text: “Leo is the onely house of the Sun, by nature, Fiery, Hot, Dry, Cholerick, Diurnal, Commanding, Bestial, Barren, of the East and Fiery Triplicity, Masculine.” (Quoted from Christian Astrology, 1647, Book I, the chapter on Leo; confidence: medium — identical wording corroborated across two independent secondary reproductions this session.)
sections.What this lens reads: 'Commanding, Bestial, Barren' packs Leo's whole 17th-century meaning into one adjective string — rulership and animality in the same breath, and barren rather than fertile — a much harsher formula than the warm, generous 'Sovereign' Leo of the modern light/shadow grammar (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical).

sections.What this lens reads: Lilly's Virgo is again marked 'barren' (as Leo is) — fertility/barrenness is a load-bearing category for him that modern astrology has almost entirely dropped in favour of psychological traits like discernment and service (compare grammars/western-astrology-canonical).
